blocks.heading: 🎨 BRIEF
blocks.text: A streaming service wants their new home screen critiqued before it ships. The client keeps saying it 'feels off' but can't tell me why. That's the job today — before you can fix a design, you have to be able to name exactly what's in it: line, shape, colour, texture, space, form. Pin those down and you can finally talk about what's actually wrong.
The elements of design: line, shape, space, texture, colour

blocks.heading: How to use this lesson
blocks.text: Work through each slide in order. Copy the definitions into your notes. Answer the two practice questions, then mark them yourself with the key.

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Understand the five elements of design and how each is used in digital products.
Success criteria

items: Identify the five elements of design in a digital product.
Describe how each element is used.
Use correct terms, not general words like "nice" or "bright".

blocks.text: Key terms

rows: A mark joining two points. Can be straight, curved, thick or thin. Used to divide, direct the eye or create a border.
A 2D area with a boundary. Geometric (circles, squares) or organic (natural forms).
The area around and between items. White (negative) space gives a design room to breathe.
How a surface looks like it would feel: rough, smooth, grainy.
Hue, value and saturation used to set mood, draw attention and link items.

blocks.text: Worked example: Elements in a streaming app home screen

blocks.html:
Look at any streaming app home screen (Netflix, Stan, Disney+). This is how the five elements are used.

Line — Thin lines separate each row of shows, so rows are easy to scan.

Shape — Rectangular thumbnails repeat across each row; round profile icons stand out from them.

Space and colour — Dark background space makes bright thumbnails stand out; red is used only for the logo and play button.

Texture — Mostly smooth and flat; some thumbnails use photographic texture to add interest.

blocks.text: Describe, do not just name

rows: Red is used only on the logo and the play button, so these stand out from the dark background.

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · LEO THORNE
blocks.text: Clients almost never complain in the language of design elements — they say 'busy' or 'boring' or 'cheap-looking'. Your job is to translate that into 'too much colour contrast' or 'not enough negative space'. Learn the vocabulary and you can diagnose a screen in thirty seconds instead of guessing.
Test tip: Elements are not principles

blocks.heading: 🔍 DESIGN REVIEW · LEO IS CHECKING YOUR WORK
blocks.text: I mark these the same way every time: name the element, then prove you saw it in the actual image, not in general. 'They used colour' earns nothing. 'They used a bright orange CTA button against a dark background to pull the eye straight to it' earns the mark.

blocks.html:
Question: Identify two elements of design in the app. (2 marks)

Earns 0 or 1 mark

"Balance and contrast." — These are principles (contrast is part of emphasis), not elements. Earns 0.

Earns full marks

"Colour and shape." — Both are elements. Only five count: line, shape, space, texture, colour.

blocks.text: A cafe menu board uses a chalkboard-look background, white hand-drawn lines between sections, round price badges, and wide gaps between the drinks and food sections.

blocks.heading: 🖌️ STUDIO CHALLENGE
blocks.text: Before I show you how I'd answer it, go find the menu board question yourself. Name three elements and, for two of them, say exactly where you see them doing work on the screen.

blocks.instruction: Tap an element of design on the left, then tap an example of it in use.

right: Divider under a heading
Round buttons on an app
Margins around text
Paper-grain background
Brand colour on all buttons

blocks.explanation: Each element of design shows up in a real product in its own characteristic way.

question.text: Identify three elements of design used in the menu board.
question.explanation:
1 mark per element
3 marks – Texture (chalkboard), line (hand-drawn dividers), shape (round badges), space (gaps between sections), colour (white on dark)

question.text: Describe how two of those elements are used.

blocks.heading: Up next
blocks.text: Next lesson: the principles of design.

blocks.heading: 🎨 BRIEF
blocks.text: A concert poster landed on my desk with a note from the client: 'make the date pop more.' That's a principles problem, not an elements one — the elements were already fine. Today's about contrast, balance, emphasis, movement, unity, proportion: the rules for how elements are arranged, not what they are.
The principles of design: balance, emphasis, dominance, unity

blocks.heading: How to use this lesson
blocks.text: Work through each slide in order. Copy the definitions into your notes. Answer the two practice questions, then mark them yourself with the key.

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Understand the four principles of design and the parts that make up emphasis and unity.
Success criteria

items: Define balance, emphasis, dominance and unity.
Identify contrast and proportion as part of emphasis, and proximity and repetition as part of unity.
Identify principles in a digital product.

blocks.text: Key terms

rows: How visual weight is spread across a design. Symmetrical (mirror image) or asymmetrical (different items with equal weight).
Making one item stand out as the focal point. Created with contrast (difference in colour, size, shape) and proportion (relative size).
Bright button on a grey page
One item is clearly the most important and is seen first, creating a visual hierarchy.
All parts look like they belong together. Created with proximity (grouping related items) and repetition (reusing colours, fonts, shapes).

blocks.text: Worked example: Principles on a concert poster

blocks.html:
A poster for a band playing at the Bunbury Entertainment Centre.

Dominance — The band photo takes up half the poster, so it is seen first.

Emphasis — The date is in bright yellow on a black background: strong contrast makes it the second focal point.

Unity — Ticket price, venue and website are grouped together at the bottom (proximity) and use the same font (repetition).

Balance — Asymmetrical: the large photo on the left is balanced by a column of text on the right.

blocks.text: What belongs where

blocks.html:
Emphasis includes — Contrast: difference in colour, size, shape or tone

Proportion: size of one item compared to another

Unity includes — Proximity: grouping related items close together

Repetition: repeating colours, fonts, shapes or layout

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · LEO THORNE
blocks.text: Elements and principles get mixed up constantly in exam answers. Quick test I give juniors: if you can point at one thing on the page and name it, it's an element (a colour, a shape). If you're describing a relationship between things — size against size, light against dark — it's a principle. Say that test to yourself before you write the answer.
Test tip: Use the syllabus names

blocks.heading: 🔍 DESIGN REVIEW · LEO IS CHECKING YOUR WORK
blocks.text: The marker wants to see you connect the principle to the actual visual effect it causes. 'Emphasis' alone is a definition. 'Emphasis, because the designer made the date the largest text on the page so it's the first thing read' is an answer that scores.

blocks.html:
Question: Identify the principle created by grouping the contact details together. (1 mark)

Earns 0 or 1 mark

"Alignment." — Alignment is a compositional rule, not a principle.

Earns full marks

"Unity (proximity)." — Proximity is part of unity, so naming unity is correct.

blocks.text: A school sports carnival flyer has a huge orange "CARNIVAL DAY" heading, a small team logo repeated in each corner, and event times grouped in one box.

blocks.heading: 🖌️ STUDIO CHALLENGE
blocks.text: Try the poster questions cold first. Match each example to its principle, then write the emphasis answer for the date — convince me it's emphasis, not just big text.

question.text: Identify the principle shown by each of: (a) the huge heading, (b) the repeated logo, (c) the grouped times.
question.explanation:
1 mark each
3 marks – (a) dominance (accept emphasis) (b) unity (repetition) (c) unity (proximity)

question.text: Describe how emphasis could be used to make the date stand out.
question.explanation:
2 marks – Describes using contrast or proportion on the date (e.g. larger, bold, in a contrasting colour to the background)
1 mark – States "make it bigger" with no link to emphasis

blocks.text: Next lesson: the relationship between elements and principles.

blocks.heading: 🎨 BRIEF
blocks.text: This is the one that trips up every junior designer I've trained: explaining how an element and a principle work together, not just naming them separately. Markers want the relationship spelled out — the answer pattern is non-negotiable, so we're drilling it until it's automatic.
Relationship between elements of design and principles of design

blocks.heading: How to use this lesson
blocks.text: Work through each slide in order. Copy the definitions into your notes. Answer the two practice questions, then mark them yourself with the key.

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Understand how elements of design are used to create principles of design.
Success criteria

items: Explain how a named element creates a named principle.
State the effect on the viewer.
Write relationship answers using the element + how + principle + effect pattern.

blocks.text: Key terms

items.definition: The way an element is used to create a principle. Elements are the tools; principles are the result.
What the relationship makes the viewer do or feel, e.g. look at the button first, see items as a group.
ELEMENT (what) + HOW it is used + creates PRINCIPLE + EFFECT on the viewer.

blocks.text: Worked example: Building a relationship answer

blocks.html:
An online shop product page has a green "Add to cart" button on a white page.

Element

Colour

How — The button is bright green while everything else is black, white and grey.

Principle — This contrast creates emphasis.

Effect — The shopper's eye goes straight to the button, so they are more likely to buy.

blocks.text: Common relationships

rows: Same brand colour on every heading
Wide gaps between sections; tight gaps within a section
Lines lead from the edge towards the product photo
Equal space on both sides of a centred logo

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · LEO THORNE
blocks.text: I make every junior memorise the pattern: name the element, name the principle, then one sentence on the effect that happens when they combine. Skip the effect and you've described two things sitting next to each other, not a relationship — and that's where marks get lost.
Test tip: Link them, do not list them

blocks.heading: 🔍 DESIGN REVIEW · LEO IS CHECKING YOUR WORK
blocks.text: I read these looking for the word 'because' or 'which creates'. If your sentence just lists the element and the principle with no causal link between them, I send it back. Show me the effect, every time.

blocks.html:
Question: Explain the relationship between one element and one principle. (3 marks)

Earns 0 or 1 mark — "The page uses colour and emphasis."

Both are named but not linked. Earns 1 mark.

Earns full marks — "The green colour of the button contrasts with the grey page, creating emphasis, so the shopper sees it first."

Element + how + principle + effect.

blocks.text: A weather app shows today's temperature in very large white numbers at the top. The next five days are shown in a row of same-sized cards below, each with the same icon style.

blocks.heading: 🖌️ STUDIO CHALLENGE
blocks.text: Have a go at both relationship questions — dominance and unity — before you check the pattern. Write them as one flowing sentence, not three separate fragments.

question.text: Explain the relationship between one element and dominance in the app.
question.explanation:
3 marks – Explains how an element (e.g. space, shape, colour) is used to make today's temperature dominant, with the effect
2 marks – Describes the element and dominance with a weak link
1 mark – Names an element or principle only

question.text: Explain the relationship between one element and unity in the app.
question.explanation:
3 marks – Explains how an element (e.g. same-sized card shapes repeated in a row) creates unity (repetition), with the effect
2 marks – Describes with a weak link
1 mark – Names only

blocks.heading: 🎨 BRIEF
blocks.text: A bus timetable app came in with white-on-pale-grey text and a client wondering why residents were complaining. Typography choices aren't decoration — on something people read standing at a bus stop in the rain, the wrong font or alignment makes the product unusable, not just unattractive.
Typography: typeface, size, alignment, format, spacing

blocks.heading: How to use this lesson
blocks.text: Work through each slide in order. Copy the definitions into your notes. Answer the two practice questions, then mark them yourself with the key.

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Understand the five parts of typography and how they affect readability.
Success criteria

items: Define the five parts of typography.
Describe typography choices in a digital product.
Justify typography choices for a given audience.

blocks.text: Key terms

rows: The design of the letters. Serif (small feet, e.g. Times New Roman) or sans serif (no feet, e.g. Arial).
How big the text is, measured in points (pt). Larger sizes create hierarchy.
How text lines up: left, right, centred or justified.
Styles applied to text: bold, italic, underline, capitals, colour.
Space between letters (kerning, tracking) and lines (leading).

blocks.text: Worked example: Typography on a bus timetable screen

blocks.html:
A digital screen at Bunbury bus station shows the next departures to people standing several metres away.

Typeface — A sans serif typeface, because it is clearer on screens and at a distance.

Size — Route numbers are the largest text so they are found first.

Alignment — Times are right-aligned in a column so the numbers line up.

Format and spacing — Bold for "Departing now"; generous line spacing so rows do not merge.

blocks.text: Common typography mistakes

blocks.html:
Avoid

More than two typefaces

Long passages in capitals — Centred body text (hard to read)

Script fonts for small text

Tight line spacing

Do — One typeface for headings, one for body

A clear size hierarchy: heading, subheading, body

Left-align body text — Bold for emphasis, not underline

Enough contrast between text and background

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · LEO THORNE
blocks.text: Justified text looks 'tidy' to a client's eye and I still have to talk them out of it on anything short — it creates ugly, uneven gaps in narrow columns, which is exactly the opposite of what they wanted. If a client pushes back, show them the gaps in their own copy.
Test tip: Name the part and give a reason

blocks.heading: 🔍 DESIGN REVIEW · LEO IS CHECKING YOUR WORK
blocks.text: Don't just name the typography choice — tie it to the audience. 'Larger font' is thin. 'A larger font size because residents reading the timetable outdoors, often at a distance or in bright sun, need it legible without squinting' is what I'd sign off.

blocks.html:
Question: Describe one typography choice for the bus screen. (2 marks)

Earns 0 or 1 mark

"Use a good font." — "Good" is not a reason and "font" is too general.

Earns full marks — "Use a sans serif typeface such as Arial, because it has no small strokes and is clearer to read from a distance."

blocks.text: A retirement village is designing a printed newsletter for its residents, many of whom have poor eyesight.

blocks.heading: 🖌️ STUDIO CHALLENGE
blocks.text: Work through the residential audience question and the justified-alignment one before you look at how I'd frame it. Say who's reading and why that changes your choice.

question.text: Describe two typography choices that would suit the residents.
Explain why justified alignment may be a poor choice for the newsletter.
question.explanation:
2 marks – Explains that justified text creates uneven gaps between words ("rivers"), which makes it harder to read
1 mark – States that it is harder to read

blocks.heading: 🎨 BRIEF
blocks.text: A photo for a website banner came in dead centre, flat, nothing drawing the eye anywhere. The fix wasn't a different photo — it was the rule of thirds, a grid, and real alignment. Compositional rules are what turn a snapshot into a banner someone actually looks at.
Compositional rules: rule of thirds, grid and alignment

blocks.heading: How to use this lesson
blocks.text: Work through each slide in order. Copy the definitions into your notes. Answer the two practice questions, then mark them yourself with the key.

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Understand how the rule of thirds, grids and alignment are used to lay out a design.
Success criteria

items: Describe the rule of thirds.
Describe how a grid and alignment organise content.
Apply compositional rules to improve a layout.

blocks.text: Key terms

items.definition: Divide the frame into a 3 x 3 grid. Place key items on the lines or where they cross, not in the dead centre.
A set of invisible columns and rows used to place content consistently.
Lining up the edges or centres of items so they look connected and organised.
The first place the eye goes; often placed on a thirds intersection.

blocks.text: Worked example: Fixing a photo for a website banner

blocks.html:
A surfer is placed in the exact centre of a wide website banner, with the text squeezed into the corner.

Problem — A centred subject looks static and leaves awkward space on both sides.

Rule of thirds — Move the surfer to the left third line, facing into the frame.

Grid — Use a 12-column grid: photo across 8 columns, text across the other 4.

Alignment — Left-align the heading, sentence and button on the same column edge.

blocks.text: Laying out a page in four steps

blocks.html:
1

Set a grid — Choose columns and margins before you place anything.

2

Place the focal point — Put the main image or heading on a thirds line.

3

Align everything — Snap text and images to the grid lines.

4

Check the space — Keep equal gaps between items of the same type.

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · LEO THORNE
blocks.text: Rule of thirds isn't 'put things slightly off-centre' — it's specific: divide the frame into a 3×3 grid and place the subject or focal point on one of those intersection lines. Vague answers lose marks here because the rule itself is precise.
Test tip: Describe, then apply

blocks.heading: 🔍 DESIGN REVIEW · LEO IS CHECKING YOUR WORK
blocks.text: I want the rule of thirds defined properly first, then applied to the actual photo — don't skip straight to 'move it left'. Tell me which line or intersection, and why that placement is stronger than centred.

blocks.html:
Question: Explain how the rule of thirds could improve the banner. (2 marks)

Earns 0 or 1 mark — "Use the rule of thirds to make it better."

Repeats the question.

Earns full marks — "Move the surfer onto the left vertical third line so the image is more interesting and the right two-thirds is free for the heading."

blocks.text: A student's Instagram post for a school play has the title, date, a photo and the ticket link all centred and stacked down the middle, with different gaps between each.

blocks.heading: 🖌️ STUDIO CHALLENGE
blocks.text: Define the rule of thirds yourself, then explain how a grid and alignment would fix the post, before you check my version.

question.text: Describe the rule of thirds.
question.explanation:
2 marks – Describes dividing the frame into a 3 x 3 grid and placing key items on the lines or intersections
1 mark – States it divides the frame into thirds

question.text: Explain how a grid and alignment could improve the post.
question.explanation:
grid (2) and alignment (2)
2 marks – Explains how a grid gives consistent positions and gaps for each item
2 marks – Explains how aligning items to one edge connects them and looks organised
- marks – Award 1 mark for each if stated without explanation

blocks.heading: 🎨 BRIEF
blocks.text: I had to walk a junior through a pizza delivery app screen this week because they kept writing 'the design is good' — zero marks, every time. Identify, describe, explain, evaluate are four different command words with four different standards, and mixing them up is the single most common way students lose marks on this course.
Identify and explain the elements and principles of design in existing digital products

blocks.heading: How to use this lesson
blocks.text: Work through each slide in order. Copy the definitions into your notes. Answer the two practice questions, then mark them yourself with the key.

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Understand how to analyse the design of an existing digital product in a structured way.
Success criteria

items: Identify elements and principles in a product.
Explain relationships between elements and principles.
Evaluate strengths and weaknesses of a design.

blocks.text: Key terms

items.definition: Name the element or principle.
Say how it is used in the product.
Say how an element creates a principle and the effect on the viewer.
Judge what works and what does not, with a reason and an improvement.

blocks.text: Worked example: Analysing a pizza delivery app screen

blocks.html:
The order screen: a large pizza photo at the top, a red "Order now" button, and menu items in a grid of same-sized cards.

Dominance — The large photo is seen first; it takes up 40% of the screen.

Emphasis — The red button contrasts with the white background, so it is the call to action.

Unity — Same-sized cards with the same font repeat across the grid.

Weakness and fix — Prices are small and pale grey. Make them bold and darker so they are easy to compare.

blocks.text: Analysis in four moves

blocks.html:
1

Scan — What do you see first, second, third?

2

Name — Which elements and principles cause that order?

3

Explain — Element + how + principle + effect.

4

Judge — One strength, one weakness, one fix.

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · LEO THORNE
blocks.text: Identify names it. Describe adds detail about how it's used. Explain adds the effect or reason — the 'why it works'. Evaluate makes a judgement with justification. If the question says 'explain' and you only describe, you've capped your own mark before the marker even reads it.
Test tip: Refer to the stimulus

blocks.heading: 🔍 DESIGN REVIEW · LEO IS CHECKING YOUR WORK
blocks.text: Check your own command word before you write a single sentence. I've sent back more exam answers for ignoring the command word than for getting the content wrong — the content was often right, just pitched at the wrong level.

blocks.html:
Question: Explain the relationship between one element and one principle in the app. (3 marks)

Earns 0 or 1 mark

"Colour creates emphasis."

True in general, but nothing from this app.

Earns full marks — "The red Order now button contrasts with the white screen, creating emphasis, so users find the button straight away."

blocks.text: A council event website home page has a full-width photo of fireworks, the event name in large white text over the photo, and four equal buttons below: Map, Food, Parking, Tickets.

question.explanation: 2 marks – Identifies an element (1) and describes its use on this page (1)

question.text: Explain the relationship between one element and unity on the page, and suggest one improvement.
question.explanation:
3 marks – Explains how an element creates unity on this page (e.g. four equal button shapes repeated in a row) with effect
2 marks – Describes with a weak link
1 mark – Names only
1 mark – Suggests a specific, relevant improvement

blocks.heading: 🎨 BRIEF
blocks.text: A flyer redesign needs two things from you by Friday: the actual modifications, and annotations explaining them to the client who can't read a mockup without commentary. This is the skill that turns 'I changed it' into something a client — or a marker — can follow and agree with.
Modify digital products to meet design needs; develop detailed annotations for digital designs

blocks.heading: How to use this lesson
blocks.text: Work through each slide in order. Copy the definitions into your notes. Answer the two practice questions, then mark them yourself with the key.

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Understand how to redesign a product to meet a brief and annotate the design clearly.
Success criteria

items: Identify what a brief requires that a draft does not provide.
Redesign a layout using elements, principles and compositional rules.
Write detailed annotations that explain each choice.

blocks.text: Key terms

items.definition: The client's requirements: purpose, audience, content and constraints.
Change an existing design so it meets the brief better.
A note on the design naming the choice, the design term and the reason or effect.
WHAT you did + DESIGN TERM + WHY or EFFECT.

blocks.text: Worked example: Annotating a redesigned flyer

blocks.html:
A draft flyer for a dog-walking business is cluttered. The brief says the phone number must be easy to find.

Layout — "Three-column grid; photo on the left third line so the eye moves right to the text."

Emphasis — "Phone number in bold orange, contrasting with the navy background, so it is the second focal point."

Unity — "Services grouped in one box (proximity) with matching paw icons (repetition)."

Typography — "One sans serif typeface; heading 36 pt, body 14 pt, left-aligned for easy reading."

blocks.text: What earns annotation marks

blocks.html:
Weak

"Nice colours"

"Logo"

"Big title"

"Picture here"

Strong — Names the element or principle

Says exactly what was done

Links it to the brief or audience

Placed next to the part it describes, with a line

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · LEO THORNE
blocks.text: A detailed annotation always has three parts: what you changed, which element or principle it uses, and why it serves the design brief. Drop any one of the three and the annotation reads like a caption, not a justification — and captions don't earn marks.
Test tip: A design with no annotations scores low

blocks.heading: 🔍 DESIGN REVIEW · LEO IS CHECKING YOUR WORK
blocks.text: I'm checking every annotation against the brief, not just against good taste. A modification can look great and still score nothing if you never connect it back to what the client actually asked for.

blocks.html:
Question: Redesign the flyer. Annotate layout, elements and principles, and typography. (12 marks)

Earns 0 or 1 mark — A neat drawing with no notes. The marker cannot award marks for reasons you did not write.

Earns full marks — A clear sketch with 8 to 10 annotations, each using the formula WHAT + TERM + WHY, and lines pointing to the part described.

blocks.text: A bakery's draft Instagram post has the logo in the centre, the opening hours in tiny text at the bottom, and five different fonts. The owner wants people to notice the new Saturday hours.

blocks.heading: 🖌️ STUDIO CHALLENGE

blocks.title: Modify and Annotate a Flyer
blocks.intro: Use the community event flyer from this lesson (or any flyer you can find online) as your starting point. You're producing two things: the modified version, and a set of detailed annotations a client could follow without seeing your working.
steps: Open the original flyer in Canva and duplicate it before making any changes, so you can show a before/after.
Identify two weaknesses using the command words from this lesson — e.g. 'the heading does not use emphasis' or 'alignment is inconsistent between the date and the venue'.

Make at least three modifications that address those weaknesses — for example, increasing the heading's size and weight for emphasis, aligning all text blocks to a single left margin, or adding negative space around the call-to-action.
Export the modified flyer as a PNG.
In a new document, write one detailed annotation per modification using the formula from this lesson: what you changed, which element or principle it uses, and why it serves the brief.
Place your before and after flyers side by side with your annotations underneath each change, pointing to exactly where on the flyer it applies.
Save your annotation document as firstname-lastname-flyer-annotations.

Write one detailed annotation for your modified design.

2 marks – Annotation names the choice, uses a design term and gives a reason or effect
1 mark – A label with a design term only

blocks.heading: 🔧 JOB TICKET
blocks.text: Call-out today: a client's laptop 'just feels slow' opening video files. Before I send a tech out, I want you to be able to explain what's actually happening inside the box — CPU, primary memory, secondary storage, volatile vs non-volatile — because half of 'it's slow' complaints are really 'you need more RAM', not a dying CPU.
Purpose of the CPU; purpose and types of memory and storage: primary, secondary

blocks.heading: How to use this lesson
blocks.text: Work through each slide in order. Copy the definitions into your notes. Answer the two practice questions, then mark them yourself with the key.

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Understand what the CPU does and the difference between primary and secondary memory.
Success criteria

items: Describe the purpose of the CPU.
Compare primary and secondary storage.
Explain how CPU and RAM specifications affect performance.

blocks.text: Key terms

items.definition: Processes instructions and performs calculations. Speed is measured in GHz; more cores means more tasks at once.
Memory the CPU uses directly. RAM is temporary (volatile): it is cleared when power is off. ROM stores start-up instructions permanently.
Stores files and programs permanently (non-volatile), e.g. SSD, HDD, USB flash drive, memory card.
Loses its data when power is turned off.

blocks.title: Inside the Computer
blocks.caption: Before the worked example, watch a file move from storage into RAM and through the CPU.

pauseQuestions.question: Name the two input devices shown, and one more input device that is not shown.
pauseQuestions.answer: Keyboard and mouse. Others include a microphone, webcam, touchscreen, scanner or game controller.

pauseQuestions.question: Why do the SSD's packets reach the RAM before the HDD's?
pauseQuestions.answer: An SSD stores data on flash memory chips with no moving parts. An HDD has to spin a disk and move a read arm to find the data, so it is much slower.

pauseQuestions.question: What happens to the data in RAM when the computer is switched off?
pauseQuestions.answer: It is lost. RAM is volatile, so it only holds data while it has power. That is why work has to be saved to storage.

pauseQuestions.question: Why do packets keep moving back and forth between the CPU and the RAM?
pauseQuestions.answer: The CPU fetches instructions and data from RAM, processes them, then writes the results back to RAM.

pauseQuestions.question: Which component turns the result into a picture? Name the two output devices shown.
pauseQuestions.answer: The graphics card (GPU) makes the picture. The output devices are the monitor and the speakers.

blocks.text: Worked example: What happens when you open a video file

blocks.html:
You double-click a video saved on your laptop.

Secondary storage — The file is stored on the SSD.

Primary memory — The file and the video player are loaded into RAM.

CPU — The CPU processes the instructions to decode and play the video.

Power off — RAM is cleared. The file is still on the SSD.

blocks.text: Primary vs secondary

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · SPARKY MILLER
blocks.text: Volatile is the word that trips people up every year. It just means 'loses its contents when the power goes' — that's RAM. Secondary storage (your SSD or hard drive) keeps everything with the power off. If a student can't tell me which one is volatile, they can't yet explain why unsaved work disappears in a blackout.
Test tip: RAM is not storage space

blocks.heading: 🧰 CALLBACK CHECK · SPARKY IS REVIEWING THE JOB
blocks.text: I grade the CPU question on function, not just the acronym — what does it actually do, in your own words, not 'it's the brain'. And for the storage comparison, I want capacity and speed both mentioned, not just one.

blocks.html:
Question: Explain why a laptop with 8 GB of RAM may be slow for video editing. (2 marks)

Earns 0 or 1 mark — "It cannot store many videos."

That is secondary storage, not RAM.

Earns full marks — "Video editing loads large clips into RAM; with only 8 GB it fills quickly, so the computer uses slower storage instead and lags."

blocks.text: A student compares two laptops for school. Laptop A: 4-core 2.4 GHz CPU, 16 GB RAM, 256 GB SSD. Laptop B: 2-core 1.6 GHz CPU, 8 GB RAM, 1 TB HDD.

blocks.heading: 🛠️ WORKSHOP CHALLENGE

question.explanation:

2 to 3 marks – Compares on one feature

blocks.text: Understand the types of peripheral devices and the three types of computer systems.

items: Classify peripherals as input, output or storage.
Describe desktop systems, mobile devices and servers.
Select a system type for a user's needs.

blocks.text: Key terms

rows: Hardware connected to a computer to add a function.
A computer at a fixed location with a separate monitor and peripherals.
A powerful computer that provides services (files, email, websites) to other computers on a network.

blocks.text: Worked example: A physiotherapy clinic

Match each person to a computer system.

Physio visiting patients — Tablet: light, battery-powered, takes notes on the move.

blocks.text: Comparing systems

rows: Fixed, often in a server room

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · SPARKY MILLER
blocks.text: The trick with tricky devices like touchscreens or multifunction printers: ask what direction the data is actually moving for the function you're thinking of. A touchscreen displays (output) and senses touch (input) — same device, two jobs. Don't force it into one box.

blocks.text: Classification questions look easy and get rushed. I send back any answer that mislabels a scanner or a server — a server in a library isn't an input or output device at all, it's a different category of machine, and conflating them tells me the concept isn't solid yet.

blocks.heading: 🔧 JOB TICKET
blocks.text: A client's asking why their old software won't run and whether Linux would save them money. That's an operating-system question dressed up as a hardware complaint — purposes of an OS, open source versus proprietary — and I need a straight answer, not a sales pitch for whichever OS I personally like.
Purpose of an operating system (OS); types of operating systems: Windows, Mac OS, iOS, Android, Linux

blocks.heading: How to use this lesson
blocks.text: Work through each slide in order. Copy the definitions into your notes. Answer the two practice questions, then mark them yourself with the key.

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Understand what an operating system does and the features of the main types.
Success criteria

items: Describe the purpose of an operating system.
Identify the device types each OS is used on.
Compare two operating systems.

blocks.text: Key terms

items.definition: Software that manages the hardware and provides a platform for applications and a user interface.
Manage memory and the CPU, manage files and storage, control peripherals (via drivers), provide a user interface, run applications, and provide security (user accounts, updates).
Source code can be viewed and changed, e.g. Linux (and the core of Android).
Owned by a company; source code is closed, e.g. Windows, macOS, iOS.

blocks.text: Worked example: Which OS where?

blocks.html:
The same person uses five operating systems in one day.

Windows — School laptop: runs most business and school software.

macOS — Graphic design studio iMac: common in creative industries.

iOS — iPhone: only on Apple mobile devices.

Android — Samsung phone and smart TV: used by many brands.

Linux — The web server hosting a website: free, stable and secure.

blocks.text: Operating systems compared

rows: Runs the widest range of software
Works closely with other Apple devices
Apps only from the App Store

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · SPARKY MILLER
blocks.text: Don't just say Linux is 'free' and proprietary is 'not free' — that's the shallow half of the answer. Free also usually means community-supported, which is an advantage for a hobbyist and a real disadvantage for a business that needs guaranteed support when something breaks at 2pm on a Tuesday.
Test tip: Purpose, not brand

blocks.heading: 🧰 CALLBACK CHECK · SPARKY IS REVIEWING THE JOB
blocks.text: For the Linux advantage/disadvantage question, I want one of each paired to this specific client, not generic textbook lines. A disadvantage that doesn't apply to their situation doesn't earn the mark even if it's true in general.

blocks.html:
Question: Describe two purposes of an operating system. (4 marks)

Earns 0 or 1 mark

"Windows and Android." — These are types, not purposes.

Earns full marks — "It manages files, so users can save, open and organise them in folders. It controls peripherals through drivers, so a printer works when plugged in."

question.explanation:

blocks.heading: 🔧 JOB TICKET
blocks.text: A practice wants new computers but is worried their current software won't run on them — or that their current software won't run on anything modern at all. Before I quote the job, I check minimum requirements both directions: can new hardware run their old software, and can an old machine run anything current.
Software compatibility issues; considerations for hardware purchase: cost, specifications, user needs; minimum hardware requirements

blocks.heading: How to use this lesson
blocks.text: Work through each slide in order. Copy the definitions into your notes. Answer the two practice questions, then mark them yourself with the key.

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Understand compatibility issues and how to choose hardware that meets software requirements and user needs.
Success criteria

items: Describe compatibility issues with older and newer software.
Compare hardware specifications against minimum requirements.
Explain purchase considerations for a user.

blocks.text: Key terms

items.definition: Whether software runs correctly on a given hardware and operating system.
May not install or may crash, because the new OS no longer supports it; no longer receives security updates.
May not install or may run slowly, because the hardware is below the minimum requirements.
The lowest specifications (CPU, RAM, storage, OS, graphics) the software needs to run.
Cost (budget), specifications (performance) and user needs (what the user will do with it).

blocks.text: Worked example: Checking minimum requirements

blocks.html:
A student wants to run a video game on her laptop.

Game needs — RAM 16 GB, 60 GB free storage, dedicated graphics card, Windows 10 64-bit or later.

Laptop has — RAM 8 GB, 200 GB free, integrated graphics, Windows 11 64-bit.

Does not meet — RAM and graphics are below the minimum.

Result — The game may not start, or run with very low frame rates.

blocks.text: Buying hardware

blocks.html:
1

User needs — What will they do? Where? How often?

2

Software — List the software and its minimum requirements.

3

Specifications — Choose specs above the minimum, with room to grow.

4

Cost — Compare options within the budget.

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · SPARKY MILLER
blocks.text: Everyone checks 'will the new software run on the old machine' and forgets the other direction — will the old, specialised software still run on new hardware and a new OS. I've seen a clinic nearly buy new PCs that couldn't run their decade-old, business-critical records software. Always check both ways.
Test tip: Compare the numbers

blocks.heading: 🧰 CALLBACK CHECK · SPARKY IS REVIEWING THE JOB
blocks.text: I'm looking for you to actually name a compatibility issue specific to this practice's setup, not recite the general definition of compatibility. And for the purchase considerations, cost alone is never a full answer — what else matters to them?

blocks.html:
Question: Identify which specifications do not meet the requirements. (2 marks)

Earns 0 or 1 mark

"It is too slow." — Does not name a specification.

Earns full marks — "RAM (8 GB is below the required 16 GB) and graphics (integrated, but a dedicated card is required)."

blocks.heading: 🔧 JOB TICKET
blocks.text: 3am call-out: a server shut itself down twice this week and the client lost power mid-task with no warning. This is exactly the job a UPS and proper environmental control exist to prevent — today's about recognising the fix before the client has to call me at 3am again.
Physical maintenance strategies (UPS, environmental temperature control) and solving simple computer problems

blocks.heading: How to use this lesson
blocks.text: Work through each slide in order. Copy the definitions into your notes. Answer the two practice questions, then mark them yourself with the key.

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Understand how to protect hardware and solve common computer problems.
Success criteria

items: Explain the purpose of a UPS and temperature control.
Describe steps to solve no sound, frozen devices and projector problems.
Apply a logical troubleshooting order.

blocks.text: Key terms

items.definition: A battery unit that keeps equipment running during a power failure long enough to save work and shut down safely. Also protects against power surges.
Keeping equipment cool with air-conditioning and ventilation, because heat damages components and causes shutdowns.
Finding and fixing a problem by checking the simplest causes first.

blocks.text: Worked example: Three common problems

blocks.html:
Check the simple things first.

No sound — Check mute and volume; check the correct output device is selected; check headphones or speaker cables; restart the app.

Frozen screen, keyboard or mouse

Wait; open Task Manager (Ctrl+Shift+Esc) and end the frozen app; check wireless mouse batteries; restart.

No display on projector — Check the cable at both ends; select the correct input on the projector; press Windows+P and choose Duplicate.

blocks.text: Why maintenance matters

blocks.html:
UPS — Server stays on during a short blackout

Time to save work and shut down safely

Stops data loss and file damage

Protects against surges

Temperature control

Servers produce a lot of heat

Overheating slows or shuts down the CPU

Heat shortens the life of components

Keep vents clear of dust

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · SPARKY MILLER
blocks.text: A UPS doesn't keep the power on forever — it buys you minutes to save your work and shut down safely, or bridges a short outage. If an answer claims a UPS 'stops the computer losing power', that's not quite it; it manages the loss, it doesn't eliminate it.
Test tip: Steps must be specific

blocks.heading: 🧰 CALLBACK CHECK · SPARKY IS REVIEWING THE JOB
blocks.text: For the blackout question I want the UPS's actual function explained, not just 'it would have helped'. And the server shutting down on hot days is a temperature problem — if your answer doesn't mention heat or cooling, you've missed what's actually being tested.

Earns 0 or 1 mark

Which settings?

Earns full marks — "Click the speaker icon and check the output is set to the laptop speakers, not a disconnected Bluetooth headset."

blocks.text: A school's referred a student case to me: under the minimum social media age, oversharing, the usual. Before I write a single recommendation I need the terms locked down properly — digital citizenship, digital footprint, social networking, the actual minimum age — because sloppy definitions sink a case review fast.
Concept of digital citizenship: responsible use of social networking

blocks.heading: How to use this lesson
blocks.text: Work through each slide in order. Copy the definitions into your notes. Answer the two practice questions, then mark them yourself with the key.

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Understand what digital citizenship means and how to use social networking responsibly.
Success criteria

items: Define digital citizenship.
Describe responsible behaviours when using social networking.
Explain the consequences of irresponsible use for the user and others.

blocks.text: Key terms

items.definition: Using digital technologies safely, responsibly and respectfully, and understanding your rights and responsibilities online.
The permanent record of everything you post, share, like and search online.
Using online platforms to create a profile, connect with others and share content.

From 10 December 2025, age-restricted social media platforms in Australia must take reasonable steps to stop under-16s having accounts. The obligation and penalties apply to platforms, not to young people or parents.

blocks.text: Worked example: Responsible or not?

blocks.html:
Jordan (17) posts about a party on Instagram. Here are four things he could do.

Posts a group photo without asking

Not responsible: others did not give permission and the photo stays in their digital footprint.

Checks privacy settings first

Responsible: only approved followers see the post.

Tags the location in real time

Risky: strangers can see where a group of young people are right now.

Deletes a friend's rude comment and messages them

Responsible: stops harm spreading and deals with it privately.

blocks.text: Responsible use of social networking

blocks.html:
Do — Think before you post: would you be happy for a future employer to see it?

Ask before posting photos of others

Use strong privacy settings

Check if information is true before you share it

Report harmful content

Avoid — Sharing your location, school or phone number publicly

Accepting requests from people you do not know

Posting while angry — Sharing other people's work without credit

Using someone else's account

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · DR ELARA FINCH
blocks.text: Digital footprint is bigger than 'what you post' — it includes what others post about you, what's logged by services, even what you deleted but was already indexed somewhere. I correct this misunderstanding in almost every case file I review.
Test tip: Explain the consequence

blocks.heading: 📝 CASE REVIEW · ELARA IS SIGNING OFF
blocks.text: Don't just define digital citizenship — the question asks for it, so give the definition cleanly, then move straight to the two behaviour changes. Vague 'be safer online' answers don't survive my sign-off; name specific, concrete changes.

Earns 0 or 1 mark

"You could get in trouble."

This is too general. It does not say how or why.

Earns full marks — "The photo becomes part of your digital footprint and can be copied or screenshotted, so it may be seen by a future employer even after you delete it."

Forms of cyberbullying, strategies to manage it, and the impact of digital technologies on work-life balance

blocks.heading: How to use this lesson
blocks.text: Work through each slide in order. Copy the definitions into your notes. Answer the two practice questions, then mark them yourself with the key.

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Understand the forms of cyberbullying, how to manage it, and how technology affects work-life balance.
Success criteria

items: Identify forms of cyberbullying.
Describe strategies to manage or limit cyberbullying.
Explain positive and negative impacts of digital technologies on work-life balance.

blocks.text: Key terms

items.definition: Using digital technology to deliberately and repeatedly hurt, threaten or embarrass someone.
Repeatedly sending offensive or threatening messages.
Deliberately leaving someone out of an online group or chat.
Pretending to be someone else online to damage their reputation.
Sharing someone's private information or images without permission.
Dividing time and energy between work and personal life in a healthy way.

blocks.text: Worked example: Managing cyberbullying

blocks.html:
A student receives abusive comments on a gaming stream every time he plays.

Do not respond — Replying usually makes it worse and gives the bully the reaction they want.

Collect evidence — Take screenshots with the date and username before anything is deleted.

Block and report — Block the accounts and report them to the platform.

Get help — Tell a trusted adult. If the platform does not act within 48 hours, report it to eSafety.

blocks.text: Work-life balance: both sides

blocks.html:
Positive impacts — Work from home saves travel time

Flexible hours around family

Stay in touch with family and friends while away

Online study at any time

Negative impacts — Always contactable: emails and messages after hours

Blurred line between work and home

Screen time replaces sleep and exercise

Less face-to-face contact can lead to isolation

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · DR ELARA FINCH
blocks.text: Each form of cyberbullying has a distinct mechanism: harassment is repeated unwanted contact, exclusion is deliberately leaving someone out, impersonation is pretending to be them, outing is exposing private information without consent. Name the mechanism, not just the umbrella term, or the strategy you recommend won't actually fit the problem.
Test tip: Answer the impact asked for

blocks.heading: 📝 CASE REVIEW · ELARA IS SIGNING OFF
blocks.text: I want the specific form identified before any strategy — a strategy for exclusion doesn't help someone being impersonated. And the work-life balance answer needs an actual impact named — lost sleep, missed family time — not just 'it's bad for her'.

blocks.heading: 📋 CASE FILE
blocks.text: A storm hit Bunbury and the local paper broke the story on social media before their own website updated. That's not a one-off — it's the whole shift from traditional publication to user-created, instantly distributed content, and it's exactly what reshaped how this industry works.
Social networking and its impact on traditional publication and distribution of information, including mobile devices

blocks.heading: How to use this lesson
blocks.text: Work through each slide in order. Copy the definitions into your notes. Answer the two practice questions, then mark them yourself with the key.

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Understand how social networking has changed the way information is published and shared.
Success criteria

items: Define social networking.
Compare traditional and social publication of information.
Explain the role of mobile devices in this change.

blocks.text: Key terms

items.definition: Online platforms where users create profiles, connect with others and share content.
Information produced and checked by publishers (newspapers, TV, radio, books) and distributed on a schedule.
How information reaches the audience: print, broadcast, or shared online.
Posts, videos and comments made by ordinary users rather than professional publishers.

blocks.text: Worked example: A storm hits Bunbury

blocks.html:
How news of a storm reaches people in 1995 and today.

1995 — A journalist writes a story, an editor checks it, and it appears in the next morning's newspaper or the 6 pm TV news.

Today — Residents post videos on Facebook and TikTok from their phones within minutes. News sites share clips from users.

Gain — Information spreads instantly and anyone can report what they see.

Loss — Posts are not checked before sharing, so false information and old videos spread too.

blocks.text: Traditional vs social

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · DR ELARA FINCH
blocks.text: The real shift isn't 'social media is faster' — it's that distribution used to be controlled by the publisher and now anyone with a phone is a distributor. That single change explains almost every follow-on impact: speed, reach, and the loss of editorial gatekeeping.
Test tip: Compare means both sides

blocks.text: I want the reason tied to distribution or user-created content specifically, not a generic 'because social media is popular'. And for the mobile devices question, name the actual impact on how people receive news, don't just restate that phones exist.

blocks.heading: 📋 CASE FILE
blocks.text: A student's in hot water for using copyrighted material and swears they thought 'private use' covered it. Half my case files are exactly this misunderstanding — the Copyright Act 1968, fair dealing, private use and moral rights don't mean what people assume they mean.
Purpose of the Copyright Act 1968 (Australia): fair dealing, private use, moral rights

blocks.heading: How to use this lesson
blocks.text: Work through each slide in order. Copy the definitions into your notes. Answer the two practice questions, then mark them yourself with the key.

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Understand what the Copyright Act 1968 protects and the exceptions that allow limited use.
Success criteria

items: State the purpose of the Copyright Act 1968.
Describe fair dealing, private use and moral rights.
Apply the Act to a scenario.

blocks.text: Key terms

items.definition: Australian law that protects creators' original works (text, images, music, film, software). Protection is automatic: no registration is needed.
Using a reasonable portion of a work without permission for specific purposes: research or study, criticism or review, parody or satire, reporting news, or professional advice.
Limited copying for your own use, e.g. copying music you own to your phone, or recording a TV show to watch later.
The creator's right to be named (attribution), not to have others named as the creator (false attribution), and not to have the work treated in a harmful way (integrity).

blocks.text: Worked example: Allowed or not?

blocks.html:
Four uses of a song by an Australian artist.

Using 20 seconds in a class video marked by your teacher

Likely fair dealing for research or study.

Uploading that video to a public YouTube channel

Not fair dealing: no longer for study. Needs permission or a licence.

Copying a song you bought to your own phone

Private use: allowed.

Remixing the song and posting it with your name as creator

Infringes copyright and the artist's moral right of attribution.

blocks.text: Common myths

blocks.html:
Myth — "It is on the internet, so it is free."

"If I credit the creator, I can use it."

"Under 10 seconds is always fine."

"I changed it a bit, so it is mine."

Fact — Online works are still protected.

Credit is required, but it is not permission.

There is no safe number of seconds; it depends on purpose and portion.

A changed work can still infringe copyright.

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · DR ELARA FINCH
blocks.text: Private use is a much narrower exception than people think — it does not mean 'I didn't make money from it' or 'I only showed my friends'. Most student infringements fail because they assumed private use covered far more than it legally does.
Test tip: Name the exception and the purpose

blocks.heading: 📝 CASE REVIEW · ELARA IS SIGNING OFF
blocks.text: Explain why this specific use infringes, don't just say 'copyright was broken'. And moral rights are a separate concept from copyright ownership — attribution and integrity of the work — so don't conflate the two in your answer.

blocks.html:
Question: Explain whether fair dealing applies. (2 marks)

Earns 0 or 1 mark — "Yes, because it is only a small part."

Size alone does not decide it.

Earns full marks — "Yes. The clip is a reasonable portion used for research or study (a school assignment), so fair dealing applies while it is only used for assessment."

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Understand how to acknowledge IP owners and reference sources in digital publications.
Success criteria

items: Explain why IP owners must be acknowledged.
Write a reference in one consistent technique (APA 7).
Acknowledge images, music and video in a digital product.

blocks.text: Key terms

items.definition: Creations of the mind, such as writing, images, music, software and designs, that belong to their creator.
Naming the creator and source of work you have used, on or with your product.
A consistent set of rules for listing sources, e.g. APA or Harvard.
A short reference in the body of the work, e.g. (eSafety Commissioner, 2026).

blocks.text: Worked example: Referencing in APA 7

blocks.html:
The same four parts appear in most references.

Website — Author. (Year). Title of page. Site name. URL

Image — Creator. (Year). Title of image [Photograph]. Site. URL

Music — Artist. (Year). Title of track [Song]. Source. URL

Video — Creator. (Year, Month Day). Title of video [Video]. YouTube. URL

blocks.text: Acknowledging in digital products

blocks.html:
Where to credit

Video: end credits — Website: caption under each image or a Credits page

Presentation: caption on the slide and a reference list

Podcast: read out and list in show notes

Creative Commons — Many free images and music use a Creative Commons licence

CC BY means you must credit the creator

NC means no commercial use

Check the licence before you use it

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · DR ELARA FINCH
blocks.text: Acknowledgement and referencing are not interchangeable terms in a marking key. Acknowledgement can be informal — a credit line. Referencing follows a specific technique, like APA 7, with exact formatting. If the question names the technique, you must use that exact format.
Test tip: A URL is not a reference

blocks.heading: 📝 CASE REVIEW · ELARA IS SIGNING OFF
blocks.text: I check APA 7 references character by character — author, year, title, source, in that specific order and punctuation. A reference with the right information in the wrong format still loses marks.

blocks.html:
Question: Write a reference for the source. (2 marks)

Earns 0 or 1 mark — "https://www.abc.net.au/news/..."

No author, date or title. Earns 0.

Earns full marks — "Smith, J. (2026). Phones in schools. ABC News. https://www.abc.net.au/news/..."

Author, year, title, site, URL.

blocks.text: Onboarded a wedding videographer this sprint and their files are a flat folder of 4,000 clips named IMG_0001 through IMG_3999. Before we can deliver anything on schedule, we need a folder structure and naming convention that a tired editor at 11pm can still navigate without guessing.
Purpose of data organisation

blocks.heading: How to use this lesson
blocks.text: Work through each slide in order. Copy the definitions into your notes. Answer the two practice questions, then mark them yourself with the key.

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Understand why data is organised and how to organise project files for a user or client.
Success criteria

items: Explain the purpose of data organisation.
Design a logical folder structure.
Apply a consistent file naming convention.

blocks.text: Key terms

items.definition: Arranging files and data in a logical, consistent way so they can be found, shared and backed up easily.
A hierarchy of folders and subfolders that groups related files.
An agreed pattern for naming files, e.g. Project_Type_Description_v01.
The letters after the dot that show the file type, e.g. .mp4, .jpg, .docx.

blocks.text: Worked example: A wedding videographer's files

blocks.html:
A videographer shoots three weddings a month and delivers files to each couple.

Folder structure — 2027 > Clients > Smith_Wedding > Footage / Audio / Graphics / Project / Exports

Naming convention — Smith_Ceremony_Cam1_001.mp4, Smith_Final_v02.mp4

Why — Any editor can find a clip in seconds, and old versions are not overwritten.

Client benefit — The couple receive a clearly named Exports folder, not 400 random files.

blocks.text: Naming rules

blocks.html:
Do — Start with the project or client name

Use underscores, not spaces

Add a version number (v01, v02)

Use dates as YYYY-MM-DD so they sort in order

Avoid — "final", "final2", "final_REAL"

Special characters like / \ : * ? " < > |

Very long names — Saving everything on the desktop

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · RORY QUINN
blocks.text: I judge a naming convention by one test: can someone who's never seen this project find the right file in under ten seconds, just from the name? If the answer's no, the convention has failed regardless of how 'organised' it looks.
Test tip: Purpose means why

blocks.heading: 🛑 STANDUP REVIEW · RORY IS CHECKING THE BOARD
blocks.text: I want a folder structure proposal that actually fits a videographer's workflow — by client, by date, by shoot type — not a generic 'Documents/Photos/Videos' template. And for the naming convention benefits, give me two that matter to a real deadline-driven business, not two restatements of 'it's tidier'.

blocks.html:
Question: Describe the purpose of data organisation for the videographer. (2 marks)

Earns 0 or 1 mark

"To keep things tidy."

Too general.

Earns full marks — "So footage for each wedding can be found quickly and is not mixed up with another couple's files, saving editing time."

blocks.text: A food truck client needs a logo that scales from a tiny Instagram icon to a 3-metre van wrap, plus a podcast episode ready for upload. Picking the right graphic and audio formats upfront saves us from re-exporting everything twice when the client asks for 'just one more size'.
Common file formats for graphics and audio: vector graphics, raster graphics, audio files

blocks.heading: How to use this lesson
blocks.text: Work through each slide in order. Copy the definitions into your notes. Answer the two practice questions, then mark them yourself with the key.

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Understand the difference between vector and raster graphics and choose suitable graphic and audio formats.
Success criteria

items: Compare vector and raster graphics.
Identify common graphic and audio file formats.
Select and justify a format for a purpose.

blocks.text: Key terms

rows: An image made of pixels. Loses quality when enlarged.
An image made of mathematical paths. Scales to any size with no loss of quality.
A file that stores sound. Formats differ in quality and file size.
Parts of an image with no background, so it sits over other content.

blocks.title: Binary Lights
blocks.caption: Raster graphics are grids of pixels stored as bytes. The last stage of this animation shows exactly that.

pauseQuestions.question: What two values can one bit hold?
How many bits are in a byte, and what is the biggest number one byte can store?
pauseQuestions.answer: 8 bits. The biggest is 11111111, which is 255.

pauseQuestions.question: Which switches would be on to show 6?
The code for B is 66. Write 66 in binary.
How many bytes does one pixel need, and what colour is 255, 0, 0?
pauseQuestions.answer: 3 bytes, one each for red, green and blue. 255, 0, 0 is pure red.

pauseQuestions.question: A photo is 4000 × 3000 pixels. Roughly how many bytes is it before compression?
pauseQuestions.answer: 12 million pixels × 3 bytes = 36 million bytes, about 36 MB. That is why formats like JPEG and PNG compress images.

blocks.text: Worked example: Choosing formats for a food truck

blocks.html:
A food truck needs files for its menu, logo, website and radio ad.

Logo — SVG: vector, so it prints sharply on the truck and on a tiny website icon.

Food photos — JPEG: small file size for photos on the website.

Logo on a photo — PNG: supports a transparent background.

Radio ad — WAV while editing (full quality); MP3 for sending (smaller file).

blocks.text: Format guide

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · RORY QUINN
blocks.text: Vector for the logo, every time, when it has to scale — it's maths, not pixels, so a van wrap and a favicon come from the exact same file with zero quality loss. Raster locks you into the resolution you exported at, and someone always asks for it bigger later.
Test tip: Format plus reason

blocks.heading: 🛑 STANDUP REVIEW · RORY IS CHECKING THE BOARD
blocks.text: Compare vector and raster on what actually matters for this client — scalability for the logo — not a generic textbook comparison. And the audio format pick needs to suit an upload platform's requirements, not just 'it's a common format'.

blocks.html:
Question: Identify a suitable format for the logo and justify it. (2 marks)

Earns 0 or 1 mark

"JPEG." — No reason, and JPEG does not scale or support transparency.

Earns full marks — "SVG, because it is a vector format, so the logo stays sharp at any size, from a business card to the side of the truck."

Open both PNG exports and compare how the small one looks — note any blurring or loss of detail.
Resize the SVG (or vector file) to 32px in your software instead, and compare its sharpness to the small PNG.

blocks.text: Key terms

rows: Changing audio: trim, cut, split, fade in or out, adjust volume, remove noise.
Fade music out at the end
Changing an audio file from one format to another.
Saving the finished edit as a new file in a chosen format and quality.
Amount of data per second of audio. Higher bit rate = better quality, larger file.

blocks.text: Worked example: Editing a voiceover

blocks.html:
A student recorded a voiceover in Audacity for a 30-second video. It has a cough, a long pause and background hum.

Trim and cut — Cut the cough and shorten the pause so the voiceover fits 30 seconds.

Noise reduction — Sample the hum and remove it from the whole track.

Volume and fades — Normalise the volume and add a short fade at the start and end.

Export — Export as WAV for the video edit, and an MP3 copy for the client to preview.

blocks.text: Audio workflow

blocks.html:
1

Import

Open or record the audio.

2

Edit — Trim, cut, fade, adjust levels, reduce noise.

3

Check — Listen through with headphones.

4

Export — Choose format and quality for the purpose.

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · RORY QUINN
blocks.text: Clients almost never flag 'the file won't open' as an editing problem, but it usually is one — sending a huge, uncompressed master file instead of exporting or converting it for delivery is the single most common reason a finished job gets stuck in someone's inbox.
Test tip: Converting is not editing

blocks.heading: 🛑 STANDUP REVIEW · RORY IS CHECKING THE BOARD
blocks.text: Name two specific editing features she'd actually use — not 'she edited it', name the tools (noise reduction, normalising volume, trimming). And explain exporting or converting as a real step with a reason, not an afterthought.

Earns 0 or 1 mark

Earns full marks — "Fade out: the volume lowers gradually at the end of the track, so the music does not stop suddenly."

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Understand how to install and update software safely.
Success criteria

items: Describe safe installation practices.
Explain the purpose of software updates.
Explain the risks of not updating software.

blocks.text: Key terms

items.definition: Copying software onto a computer and setting it up so it can run.
A new version of installed software that fixes bugs, closes security holes or adds features.
A small update that fixes a specific problem, often a security weakness.
Permission needed to install software on many computers, to stop unwanted programs being installed.

blocks.text: Worked example: Installing software at school

blocks.html:
A teacher wants Audacity on 30 school laptops.

Check requirements — Confirm the laptops meet the minimum requirements.

Trusted source — Download only from the official site or the school's software centre.

Licence — Check it is free for schools (Audacity is open source).

Deploy — IT installs it with administrator rights on all 30 laptops at once.

blocks.text: Why update?

blocks.html:
Updates give you — Security fixes that stop malware using known weaknesses

Bug fixes so the software crashes less

New features — Compatibility with new operating systems and files

Not updating risks — Malware exploiting old security holes

Crashes and lost work

Files that will not open

No support from the developer

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · RORY QUINN
blocks.text: Ignoring updates isn't a convenience trade-off, it's a security decision whether people realise it or not — most patches exist specifically to close a vulnerability that's already being exploited somewhere. 'I'll do it later' on an update is a risk decision, say it plainly.
Test tip: Security is the key reason

blocks.heading: 🛑 STANDUP REVIEW · RORY IS CHECKING THE BOARD

Earns 0 or 1 mark

"To get the newest version."

Earns full marks — "Updates patch security weaknesses that hackers know about, so the computer is less likely to be infected with malware."

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Understand the types of software licences and what each allows users to do.
Success criteria

items: Define open source, closed source, proprietary, shareware and freeware.
Compare two licence types.
Recommend a licence type for a user.

blocks.text: Key terms

rows: A legal agreement setting out how software can be used, copied and shared.
Source code is available to view, change and share, usually free.
Source code is kept secret by the owner.
Owned by a company; users pay for a licence and must follow its rules.
Free to try for a limited time or with limited features, then you pay.
Free to use but closed source; the owner keeps copyright.

blocks.text: Worked example: Choosing software for a community group

blocks.html:
A volunteer surf club needs photo editing software on two old laptops with no budget.

Proprietary (Photoshop) — Best features but a paid subscription: not in the budget.

Shareware — Free trial ends after 7 days: not a long-term option.

Freeware — Free but limited features and cannot be changed.

Open source (GIMP) — Free, legal on both laptops, community support: best fit.

blocks.text: Licences compared

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · RORY QUINN
blocks.text: Proprietary software usually buys guaranteed support and regular updates for a price; the free or open alternative buys flexibility and zero licence cost but often means the group is on their own when something breaks. Neither is automatically the right call — it depends on whether this group has anyone technical enough to self-support.
Test tip: Freeware is not open source

blocks.heading: 🛑 STANDUP REVIEW · RORY IS CHECKING THE BOARD
blocks.text: Define proprietary software precisely first. Then the comparison for this school needs both options weighed against their actual situation — budget, technical skill available — not a generic pros-and-cons list.

Earns 0 or 1 mark

"Both are free." — One similarity, no difference.

Earns full marks — "Both are usually free, but open source lets users view and change the source code, while freeware is closed source, so only the owner can change it."

blocks.text: A sports club's membership spreadsheet has prices stored as text in some rows and numbers in others — their totals formula is broken and nobody can see why. Spreadsheet design isn't decoration, it's the difference between a sheet that calculates correctly and one that silently gives wrong answers.
Composition, layout and design considerations for construction of spreadsheets

blocks.heading: How to use this lesson
blocks.text: Work through each slide in order. Copy the definitions into your notes. Answer the two practice questions, then mark them yourself with the key.

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Understand how to lay out a spreadsheet so data is clear, accurate and easy to use.
Success criteria

items: Describe layout and design considerations for spreadsheets.
Apply consistent formatting to a spreadsheet.
Explain how a design choice helps the user.

blocks.text: Key terms

items.definition: The first row naming each column. Bold and frozen so it stays visible when scrolling.
Each column holds one kind of data (dates, prices, names) so it can be sorted and calculated.
How values display: currency, percentage, date, decimal places.
Locks rows or columns so headings stay on screen.
Changes a cell's colour automatically based on its value, e.g. red if stock is below 5.

blocks.text: Worked example: A sports club membership sheet

blocks.html:
A club treasurer keeps 200 members in one sheet. It was hard to read, so she redesigned it.

Before — No headings, merged cells, fees typed as "fifty dollars", dates in different styles.

Headings — Row 1: Surname, First name, Team, Fee paid, Date paid. Bold and frozen.

Formats — Fee as currency ($50.00); dates as DD/MM/YYYY; column widths fit the data.

Conditional formatting — Unpaid fees turn light red, so the treasurer sees them instantly.

blocks.text: Design checklist

blocks.html:
Layout — Headings in row 1, data from row 2

No blank rows or columns inside the data

No merged cells inside the data

Totals below or beside the data, clearly labelled

Formatting — Consistent number and date formats

Bold headings, frozen panes

Alternating row shading or borders for readability

Colour used for meaning, not decoration

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · RORY QUINN
blocks.text: A heading row, one data type per column, and a consistent number format aren't style preferences — they're what makes formulas and sorting actually work. Mixed text and numbers in one 'price' column is the single most common reason a club treasurer's totals don't add up.
Test tip: Say how it helps the user

blocks.heading: 🛑 STANDUP REVIEW · RORY IS CHECKING THE BOARD
blocks.text: Explain why consistent number formatting matters for this exact problem — calculations silently breaking — not formatting in general. And give two other layout improvements that would genuinely help this specific sheet, not a generic spreadsheet checklist.

blocks.html:
Question: Describe one layout consideration for the membership sheet. (2 marks)

Earns 0 or 1 mark

"Make it look nice."

Not a layout consideration.

Earns full marks — "Freeze the heading row so the treasurer can still see what each column means when she scrolls down to member 150."

blocks.heading: 🎟️ TICKET
blocks.text: Same membership sheet, new request: the club wants beginners under 18 pulled out for a new program, fast, without touching the master list. That's a filter job, not a sort job — and knowing which tool solves which problem is exactly what separates a ten-second fix from a messy manual search.
Organisation and management of data using sort filters in spreadsheets

blocks.heading: How to use this lesson
blocks.text: Work through each slide in order. Copy the definitions into your notes. Answer the two practice questions, then mark them yourself with the key.

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Understand how sorting and filtering help users find and organise data.
Success criteria

items: Distinguish between sorting and filtering.
Apply single and multi-level sorts.
Apply filters to show only the data needed.

blocks.text: Key terms

items.definition: Reorders all rows by one or more columns, ascending (A to Z, smallest first) or descending.
Sorts by one column, then by a second within it, e.g. Team, then Surname.
Temporarily hides rows that do not match a condition. The data is not deleted.
The rule a row must meet to be shown, e.g. Fee paid = No, or Score greater than 80.

blocks.text: Worked example: Using the membership sheet

blocks.html:
The treasurer needs three lists from the same 200 members.

Alphabetical list — Sort by Surname A to Z, then First name A to Z.

Each team's list — Sort by Team, then Surname, so each team is grouped in order.

Who has not paid — Filter Fee paid to show only "No".

Under 12s who have not paid

Two filters: Team = Under 12 and Fee paid = No.

blocks.text: Sort or filter?

rows: Rank players from highest to lowest score
Show only players in the Under 14 team
Group by team, then alphabetical within each team
Show only scores above 80, highest first

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · RORY QUINN
blocks.text: Sort rearranges everything permanently (until you sort again); filter temporarily hides rows that don't match, leaving the underlying data untouched. If the club needs to find a subgroup without disturbing the master list for everyone else, filter is always the right tool, not sort.
Test tip: Filtering hides, it does not delete

blocks.heading: 🛑 STANDUP REVIEW · RORY IS CHECKING THE BOARD
blocks.text: Describe a multi-level sort as an actual layered rule — sort by this, then by that — not just 'sort the data'. And the filter answer needs the specific condition that pulls beginners under 18, named precisely.

blocks.html:
Question: Describe the difference between sorting and filtering. (2 marks)

Earns 0 or 1 mark

"Filtering removes data." — Filtered rows are only hidden.

Earns full marks — "Sorting changes the order of all rows; filtering hides rows that do not meet a condition without deleting them."
