blocks.text: Bunbury Surf Club wants a Nippers sign-up reel and the deadline's tight — before I let anyone touch a camera, we run through the four project management considerations. Skip this step and the first thing that gets sacrificed under pressure is quality, every single time.
Project management considerations: scope, time, resources, client brief

blocks.heading: How to use this lesson
blocks.text: Work through each slide in order. Write the definitions and the table into your notes. Answer the two practice questions, then mark them yourself with the key.

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Understand how scope, time, resources and the client brief shape the planning of a digital product.
Success criteria

items: Define each of the four project management considerations using syllabus wording.
Outline how each consideration applies to a given scenario.
Explain how a change to one consideration affects the others.

blocks.text: The four considerations

rows: What the project will and will not produce: the features, content and size of the final product.
What exactly am I making? What is not included?
The deadlines and the time available to complete each stage of the project.
When is it due? How long will each stage take?
The people, hardware, software, money and materials needed to complete the project.
Who and what do I need? What will it cost?
The client's written requirements: purpose, audience, content and any constraints.
What has the client asked for? What must I include?

blocks.text: Worked example: Bunbury Surf Club: Nippers sign-up reel

blocks.html:
The surf club wants a 30-second video reel for Instagram to promote its Nippers sign-up day in three weeks. Volunteers have one phone and a free editing app. The club has no budget.

Scope — One 30-second reel for Instagram. A poster or website is not part of this project.

Time — Three weeks until sign-up day, so filming must be done in week 1 and editing in week 2, leaving week 3 for feedback.

Resources — One phone, a free editing app and volunteer time. No money for music, so only royalty-free tracks.

Client brief — Promote the sign-up day to parents of 5 to 13 year olds; must show the date, the club logo and how to register.

blocks.text: Change one, and the others move

blocks.html:
Scope

Time

Resources

Client brief — The client brief sits in the middle: every decision must still meet it.

Less time: reduce the scope (a 15-second reel) or add resources (another editor).

Bigger scope: add a poster and you need more time or more people.

Fewer resources: no budget means free software and your own footage, which can take longer.

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · RORY QUINN
blocks.text: The four considerations fight each other by design — more time or more budget buys better quality, but real projects rarely get more of either. Naming the trade-off honestly up front is worth more than pretending you can max out all four at once.
Test tip: Link every answer to the scenario

blocks.heading: 🛑 STANDUP REVIEW · RORY IS CHECKING THE BOARD
blocks.text: Outline all four considerations for this reel specifically, not a generic list. And for the 10-second ad add-on, I want you to say which consideration gets squeezed when scope increases but the deadline doesn't move.

blocks.html:
Earns 0 or 1 mark — Time is how long the project takes.

This is a definition. It does not say anything about the scenario, so it cannot earn the "outline how it applies" mark.

Earns full marks — The reel is due in three weeks, so filming must be finished in week 1 to leave time for editing and club feedback.

This uses a detail from the scenario (three weeks) and shows the effect on the project.

Add a short paragraph: the manager has now asked for a 10-second ad added. State which consideration gets squeezed and by how much (e.g. '2 extra days needed, or quality drops on the original three scenes').

blocks.heading: Lesson objective

Success criteria

items: Define product purpose, design criteria, target audience characteristics and presentation medium.
Write design criteria that are specific and can be checked.

blocks.text: Key terms

rows: What the digital product must achieve for the client (e.g. inform, persuade, entertain, sell).
Inform parents about a school camp
Specific, checkable statements the finished product will be judged against.
Camp date appears on every page

Parents aged 35 to 55, reading on phones

blocks.text: Worked example: Bunbury Library: school holiday program

blocks.html:
The library wants a product that tells families about free school holiday workshops for children aged 8 to 12. Most parents check the library's Facebook page on their phones.

Purpose — Inform families about the workshops and persuade them to book a place.

Target audience — Parents aged 30 to 50 reading on phones; children aged 8 to 12 who will look at the pictures.

Presentation medium — A square social media image post, because parents already follow the Facebook page on their phones.

Design criteria — Workshop dates and booking link are readable on a phone screen. No more than 40 words of text. Library logo appears in the same corner as other library posts.

blocks.text: Good criteria can be checked

blocks.html:
Vague (earns 0)

Looks good

Is colourful

Is easy to use

Appeals to kids

Specific and checkable — Uses the three library brand colours only

Date and time are in the largest text after the heading

Readable on a 6-inch phone screen without zooming

Includes one photo of children at a workshop

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · RORY QUINN
blocks.text: Design criteria that aren't testable are useless to a project manager — 'make it fun' can't be checked off at the end. 'Under 90 seconds, features at least three activities, suitable for ages 6 to 12' can actually be verified against the finished product.
Test tip: Criteria must be measurable

blocks.heading: 🛑 STANDUP REVIEW · RORY IS CHECKING THE BOARD
blocks.text: Describe two real characteristics of this specific audience — age, what motivates holiday program sign-ups — not generic audience traits. And I want three design criteria that are genuinely measurable, not three vague wishes.

rows: A small, quick sketch used to try out many layout ideas fast.
Six poster layouts on one page

blocks.text: Worked example: Planning an animated safety message

blocks.html:
A council wants a 15-second animation reminding people to swim between the flags.

Annotated sketch — A detailed drawing of the final frame with labels for colour, font and logo position.

Annotated notes — Notes recording the council's feedback and why the opening was changed.

blocks.text: Annotation: label vs explain

blocks.html:
A label (weak)

"Blue"

"Big heading"

"Logo here"

An annotation (strong) — "Blue matches the council brand and creates unity with other council posts"

"Heading is 3x the body size so it is dominant"

"Logo top-left, where other council posts put it"

blocks.text: Thumbnails exist to let you fail fast and cheap — a bad sequence idea costs ten seconds to scrap on paper and hours to scrap once it's animated. Any team that skips straight to production because 'we know what we want' ends up redoing more work than they saved.

blocks.text: The school canteen ordering page shipped and now it needs evaluating — properly, against criteria, with actual evidence, not just 'yeah it's fine'. Evaluation is the step every rushed project skips, and it's exactly the step that tells you whether to do it the same way next time.

items: Identify the types of criteria used to evaluate a product.
Describe methods for gathering evaluation evidence.
Write an evaluation that uses evidence.

blocks.text: Key terms

items.definition: Judging how well a finished product meets its purpose, brief and design criteria, using evidence.

Proof used in an evaluation: user feedback, client comments, test results, screenshots.

blocks.text: Worked example: Evaluating a school canteen ordering page

blocks.html:
The design criteria were: menu loads on a phone in under 3 seconds; allergy symbols on every item; order in 4 taps or fewer.

Criterion met — Menu loaded in 2 seconds on three different phones (tested).

Criterion partly met — Allergy symbols appear on hot food but not on drinks. Fix: add to drinks.

Criterion not met — Ordering took 6 taps in user testing. Fix: add a "Quick order" button.

Evidence used — Timed tests, a survey of 10 students and feedback from the canteen manager.

blocks.text: Ways to gather evidence

rows: What the audience thinks, with ratings you can count
What people actually do and where they get stuck
Whether the brief has been met
What you would change and what you learned

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · RORY QUINN
blocks.text: Self-reflection without evidence is just an opinion with extra steps. 'I think it worked well' earns nothing from a marker or a client — a screenshot of actual usage, a user comment, a measured outcome is what turns an opinion into an evaluation.

blocks.heading: 🛑 STANDUP REVIEW · RORY IS CHECKING THE BOARD
blocks.text: Name two real methods for gathering evidence on this page — a user survey, usage data, direct observation — not 'I would ask people'. And I want two more design criteria that are genuinely testable against the finished product, matching the standard from earlier in this topic.

blocks.text: Key terms

items.definition: Adjusting a file's size, resolution, format and colour so it suits where it will be used, with the smallest size that still looks right.
Detail in an image. Print is measured in pixels per inch (ppi); screens use pixel dimensions (e.g. 1920 x 1080).
Needs high resolution (about 300 ppi) and CMYK colour, so files are large.

blocks.text: Worked example: One photo, three uses

Email to a buyer — Resized to 1200 pixels wide so it fits under attachment limits.

Fast pages keep buyers on the site; sharp prints look professional.

blocks.text: Print vs online

rows: Pixel size to fit the screen

blocks.text: Two files, two very different compression needs crossed my desk this week — and picking the wrong type for the wrong job either wrecks the quality or barely shrinks the file. blocks.text: Key terms

rows: Reducing file size so data transfers faster and uses less storage.
Permanently removes some data the user is unlikely to notice. Much smaller files; quality can drop.
Reduces size without losing any data; the original can be restored exactly.
How much storage a file uses: KB, MB, GB.

blocks.text: Worked example: Choosing compression

blocks.html:
Four files a designer needs to send.

Holiday photos for Instagram

Lossy (JPEG): small files, quality loss not noticed on a phone.

Client's logo with text — Lossless (PNG): sharp edges and text stay crisp.

Folder of contracts — Lossless (ZIP): every character must be exactly the same.

Music for streaming — Lossy (MP3/AAC): small enough to stream smoothly.

blocks.text: Lossy vs lossless

rows: Can drop, especially if saved repeatedly
Small size matters more than perfect quality

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · SLOANE VANE
blocks.text: My rule of thumb: if the file needs to be restored byte-for-byte identical — a document, a database export — it's lossless, no exceptions. If it's a photo or audio where a human eye or ear won't notice the difference, lossy buys you a much smaller file for free.

blocks.text: State the purpose of compression cleanly first. Then for each use, I want the type named and justified against what that specific use actually needs — quality-critical or size-critical — not just 'lossy is smaller'.

Earns full marks — "Lossy permanently removes data, so files like JPEG are much smaller but lower quality; lossless keeps all the data, so PNG or ZIP files can be restored exactly but are larger."

blocks.heading: 🎟️ TICKET
blocks.text: A website photo needs cropping to fit a banner, and a PDF is bloated because nobody resampled the images inside it before export. Cropping and resampling get confused constantly — one changes what's in the frame, the other changes how much data describes it.
Techniques for file size minimisation: cropping, resampling

blocks.heading: How to use this lesson
blocks.text: Work through each slide in order. Copy the definitions into your notes. Answer the two practice questions, then mark them yourself with the key.

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Understand how cropping and resampling reduce image file sizes.
Success criteria

items: Describe cropping and resampling.
Explain how each reduces file size.
Apply both to prepare an image for a product.

blocks.text: Key terms

items.definition: Removing unwanted areas from the edges of an image. Fewer pixels, smaller file, and a stronger composition.
Changing the number of pixels in an image. Downsampling reduces the pixel dimensions and file size.
Width x height in pixels, e.g. 6000 x 4000.
Adding pixels. Makes the file larger and the image blurry; avoid it.

blocks.text: Worked example: Preparing a website photo

blocks.html:
A 6000 x 4000 pixel photo (8 MB) of a cafe owner needs to fit a 1200 x 800 website box.

Step 1: crop — Remove the empty car park on the left; the owner is now on a thirds line. 4500 x 3000 pixels.

Step 2: resample — Downsample to 1200 x 800 pixels.

Step 3: export

JPEG at 75% quality.

Result — About 200 KB: 40 times smaller, and it looks the same on screen.

blocks.text: Order matters

blocks.html:
1

Keep the original — Work on a copy; resampling down cannot be undone.

2

Crop first

Remove what you do not need.

3

Resample — Reduce to the size it will display at.

4

Export

Choose format and quality.

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · SLOANE VANE
blocks.text: Cropping removes part of the image — the pixel dimensions and framing both change. Resampling reduces the number of pixels describing the same framing — the content stays, the detail shrinks. Confuse the two in an answer and I know immediately the concept isn't understood, just the word.
Test tip: Say why the file gets smaller

blocks.heading: 🛑 PR REVIEW · SLOANE IS AUDITING YOUR WORK
blocks.text: Describe cropping's specific effect on this photo, not the definition in isolation. And for resampling reducing the PDF's size — I want 'fewer pixels, smaller file' explained, not just asserted.

blocks.html:

Earns 0 or 1 mark — "It makes the picture smaller."

Does not mention pixels.

Earns full marks — "Resampling reduces the number of pixels, e.g. from 6000 wide to 1200 wide, so there is much less data to store."

Save this as Version-B and compare its file size to Version-A.

items.definition: Organising, storing, sharing and protecting files kept online (e.g. OneDrive, Google Drive).
An online folder that set people can open, with chosen permissions.
Who can view, comment or edit a file or folder.

blocks.text: Worked example: A netball club's online files

blocks.html:
Five committee members share files on OneDrive.

Structure — One shared "Club 2027" folder with subfolders: Finance, Teams, Fixtures, Photos.

Organise

Logical folder structure

Consistent file names

Archive old files

Delete duplicates

Share and protect — Share links with the least permission needed

Remove access when people leave

Turn on two-step verification

Check sync before working offline

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · SLOANE VANE
blocks.text: Most 'someone deleted my file' disasters are actually a permissions failure, not malice — give everyone full edit access to everything and eventually someone will overwrite or delete work they didn't mean to touch. Tiered permissions aren't bureaucracy, they're damage control.

blocks.heading: 🎟️ TICKET
blocks.text: A club newsletter went through six 'final' versions and nobody can find which one actually got sent. blocks.text: Key terms

items.definition: Managing changes to a document so the current version is clear and earlier versions can be found or restored.
Adding v01, v02 to file names; major changes can use v1.0, v2.0.
A record kept by OneDrive or Google Docs of every saved version, which can be viewed or restored.
The single, official current version of a document.
Locking a file while one person edits it, so others cannot overwrite changes.

blocks.text: Worked example: Writing a club newsletter

blocks.html:
The newsletter editor and two writers work on the same document each month.

One master copy — Stored in the shared folder; nobody emails attachments.

Version history — When a paragraph is deleted by mistake, the editor restores yesterday's version.

Naming — Newsletter_2027-06_v03 when saving a copy for the printer.

Comments — Writers suggest changes as comments; the editor accepts or rejects them.

blocks.text: Good and bad version control

Bad

report_final2.docx

Good — Report_v01.docx, Report_v02.docx

Dates in YYYY-MM-DD format

One shared master with version history

blocks.heading: How to use this lesson

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Understand how maintenance utility tools keep a computer running efficiently.
Success criteria

items: Describe disk clean-up, temporary file and cache deletion, and defragmentation.
Explain how each improves performance.
Identify when defragmentation should not be used.

blocks.text: Key terms

items.definition: Software that maintains or protects the computer rather than doing a user task.
Finds and removes unneeded files (temporary files, recycle bin, old updates) to free storage space.
Files programs create while working; many are left behind and waste space.
Copies of web pages and images saved by the browser so sites load faster. Clearing it frees space and can fix display errors.
Parts of a file are scattered across a hard disk drive, so it takes longer to read. Defragmentation rearranges them. Not needed on SSDs; Windows optimises SSDs differently.

blocks.text: Worked example: Fixing a slow family computer

blocks.html:
A 6-year-old desktop with a hard disk drive is slow and has only 2 GB free.

Disk clean-up — Removes 18 GB of old update files and temporary files.

Clear browser cache — Frees 3 GB and fixes a website that shows old images.

Defragment — The HDD is 30% fragmented; defragmenting makes files open faster.

Result — More free space, faster start-up and file opening.

blocks.text: Which tool fixes what?

rows: Website shows old content or errors
Files slow to open on an old HDD

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · SLOANE VANE
blocks.text: Defragmentation is the classic trap question — it's essential on an old spinning hard drive and actively unnecessary, even mildly harmful, on an SSD, which have no moving parts to benefit from it. If a laptop has an SSD, say so and explain why defrag doesn't apply.
Test tip: Say how it improves performance

blocks.heading: 🛑 PR REVIEW · SLOANE IS AUDITING YOUR WORK
blocks.text: Name two specific utility tools and what each actually fixes for this laptop, not a generic list of 'things that help'. And if it's an SSD, don't recommend defrag — explain why it's not needed, that's the actual mark.

blocks.intro: Actually run the maintenance utilities from this lesson on a real computer and report genuine findings — not hypothetical ones.
steps: On Windows, open Disk Cleanup (search for it in the Start menu) or on Mac, open About This Mac > Storage > Manage. Record how much space it reports could be freed.

blocks.text: Key terms

items.definition: Any software designed to harm a computer or steal data. Includes viruses, spyware, ransomware and trojans.
Malware that attaches to files and spreads when they are opened or shared.
Malware that secretly collects information such as passwords, browsing and keystrokes.

blocks.text: Worked example: A suspicious email

blocks.html:

If opened — The attachment contains spyware that records passwords.

blocks.text: Staying protected

Tools — Anti-malware with real-time scanning (e.g. Microsoft Defender)

Spam filter in the email service

Firewall turned on

Automatic updates

Habits — Do not open unexpected attachments

Hover over links to check the address

Download software only from official sites

Use strong, different passwords

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · SLOANE VANE
blocks.text: A virus and spyware aren't the same threat even though people lump them together — a virus spreads and disrupts, spyware quietly watches and steals information without the user noticing anything's wrong at all. Misname the malware type and your recommended fix won't match the actual problem.

blocks.text: Understand what a computer network is, why it is used, and its advantages and disadvantages.
Success criteria

items: Explain the concept and purpose of a computer network.
Describe advantages of networking.
Describe disadvantages of networking.

blocks.text: Key terms

items.definition: Two or more devices connected so they can share data and resources.
A network in one building or site, e.g. a home, school or office.
A network over a large area. The internet is the largest WAN.
Hardware, software, files and an internet connection used by many devices on the network.

blocks.title: Packet Journey
blocks.caption: See a network in action before you work through the home network example.

pauseQuestions.question: Why is the message split into packets instead of being sent in one piece?
pauseQuestions.answer: Small packets share the network fairly, can take different routes, and if one is lost only that packet has to be sent again.

pauseQuestions.question: What is the job of the switch?
pauseQuestions.answer: It connects the devices inside one local network (LAN) and sends each packet to the right device.

pauseQuestions.question: What does the router do that the switch does not?
pauseQuestions.answer: It connects different networks, such as the school network and the internet. It reads each packet's destination address to decide where to send it.

pauseQuestions.question: Why do the packets arrive in the order 3, 1, 4, 2?
pauseQuestions.answer: Each packet can take a different route. Some routes are shorter or less busy, so the packets arrive out of order.

pauseQuestions.question: How does Sam's laptop rebuild the message in the right order?
pauseQuestions.answer: Every packet is numbered, so the laptop puts them back in number order.

pauseQuestions.question: What happens if one packet never arrives?
pauseQuestions.answer: Sam's laptop never confirms it, so your laptop sends that packet again.

blocks.text: Worked example: A home network

blocks.html:
A family of four with phones, laptops, a smart TV and a printer.

Share the internet — One NBN connection for every device.

Share hardware — Everyone prints to one wireless printer.

Share files — Family photos on a shared drive.

Communicate — Stream from a phone to the TV; play games together.

blocks.text: Networking

blocks.html:
Advantages — Share one internet connection and printer, saving money

Share files without USB drives

Central backup of files — Communication and collaboration

Disadvantages — Malware can spread to every device

Security risks from unauthorised access

If the router fails, nobody has internet

Setup and maintenance cost and skill

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · SPARKY MILLER
blocks.text: When a client asks 'why network it', the honest answer is almost always one of: sharing a printer, sharing files, or sharing an internet connection. If your explanation doesn't land on one of those practical benefits, it's too abstract to convince anyone to pay for the job.
Test tip: Advantage plus effect

blocks.heading: 🧰 CALLBACK CHECK · SPARKY IS REVIEWING THE JOB
blocks.text: I want the office's actual networking purpose named, not a textbook definition of 'network'. And for advantage/disadvantage, a disadvantage like 'cost' needs to be specific to this setup, not a throwaway line.

blocks.heading: 🔧 JOB TICKET
blocks.text: A client wants their shed connected to the house network and is asking whether wifi will just reach. Depends entirely on the medium — optic fibre, twisted pair, wireless — and each one has a job it's genuinely good at and a job it'll fail at. I've seen too many wireless-only sheds with constant dropouts.
Types of transmission media: optic fibre, wired, wireless

blocks.heading: How to use this lesson
blocks.text: Work through each slide in order. Copy the definitions into your notes. Answer the two practice questions, then mark them yourself with the key.

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Understand the three types of transmission media and when each is used.
Success criteria

items: Describe optic fibre, wired and wireless media.
Compare transmission media on speed, distance, interference and mobility.
Select media for a location in a network.

blocks.text: Key terms

items.definition: The physical path data travels along between devices.
Glass or plastic strands carrying data as pulses of light. Very fast, long distances, no electrical interference.
Copper Ethernet cable (e.g. Cat6) carrying electrical signals. Fast and reliable, up to about 100 m.
Radio waves (Wi-Fi). Devices can move around, but walls, distance and other devices reduce speed.

blocks.text: Worked example: Media in a school

blocks.html:
Each medium used where it fits best.

Optic fibre — Between buildings and from the street to the school: long distance, high speed.

Wired Ethernet — Desktop computers in the library and servers: fast and reliable.

Wireless — Student laptops in classrooms: students move between rooms.

Why mix?

Each medium suits a different need for speed, distance and mobility.

blocks.text: Comparing media

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · SPARKY MILLER
blocks.text: Distance and obstacles are the two things that kill wireless every time, and clients never think about either until it's already failed. For anything outdoors or through brick, I default to recommending a wired run even when it's a harder sell upfront — it saves me a callback.
Test tip: Compare both sides

blocks.heading: 🧰 CALLBACK CHECK · SPARKY IS REVIEWING THE JOB
blocks.text: A recommendation without a reason tied to distance, obstacles or cost isn't a recommendation, it's a guess that happened to be right. Justify the medium against this specific shed-to-house distance, not media in general.

blocks.html:
Question: Compare wired and wireless media for a home office. (4 marks)

Earns 0 or 1 mark

"Wireless is easier."

One side, no feature.

Earns full marks — "Wired Ethernet is faster and more reliable for the desktop because walls do not affect it, but wireless lets the laptop move around the house without cables."

blocks.heading: 🔧 JOB TICKET
blocks.text: A client on a 100/20 plan keeps asking why their evening live stream keeps freezing when their speed test says 100. Transmission rate, upload versus download, and bandwidth explain exactly why a fast-looking plan can still choke — and it's rarely the plan's fault alone.
Concept of transmission rates

blocks.heading: How to use this lesson
blocks.text: Work through each slide in order. Copy the definitions into your notes. Answer the two practice questions, then mark them yourself with the key.

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Understand transmission rates and how they affect what users can do on a network.
Success criteria

items: Explain the concept of transmission rate.
Convert between units: bps, Mbps, Gbps.
Explain how upload and download rates affect a task.

blocks.text: Key terms

items.definition: The amount of data sent per second, measured in bits per second (bps).
1 Mbps = 1 million bits per second; 1 Gbps = 1000 Mbps. Note: 8 bits = 1 byte, so 100 Mbps is about 12.5 MB per second.
Speed of data coming to your device, e.g. streaming, downloading.
Speed of data leaving your device, e.g. sending files, video calls. Home plans usually upload much slower than they download.
The maximum rate a connection can carry; shared by every device using it.

blocks.text: Worked example: A 100/20 home plan

blocks.html:
An NBN plan with 100 Mbps download and 20 Mbps upload.

Streaming 4K — Needs about 25 Mbps download: easy.

Uploading a 2 GB video — 2 GB = 16 000 megabits. At 20 Mbps: about 800 seconds, or 13 minutes.

Four people at once — The 100 Mbps is shared, so each device gets less.

Wi-Fi limit — A weak signal in the back bedroom may only reach 30 Mbps.

blocks.text: Working out a transfer time

blocks.html:
1

Size in bytes

e.g. 2 GB = 2000 MB.

2

Convert to bits

x 8 = 16 000 megabits.

3

Divide by rate

16 000 / 20 Mbps = 800 s.

4

Convert

800 s is about 13 minutes.

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · SPARKY MILLER
blocks.text: Download and upload rates are almost never the same number, and a live stream depends on upload — the number everyone forgets to check. 100/20 means 100 down, 20 up; if you're uploading video, that 20 is your real ceiling, not the headline 100.
Test tip: Bits are not bytes

blocks.heading: 🧰 CALLBACK CHECK · SPARKY IS REVIEWING THE JOB
blocks.text: Explain transmission rate properly first — units, what's being measured — before you diagnose the freezing. And for 'why does it freeze in the evening', I want congestion or shared bandwidth mentioned, not just 'the internet is slow'.

blocks.html:
Question: Explain how the upload rate affects sending a large video. (2 marks)

Earns 0 or 1 mark

"It will be slow." — No link to the rate or the task.

Earns full marks — "The upload rate is only 20 Mbps, so a 2 GB video takes about 13 minutes to send; a faster upload rate would reduce this time."

blocks.heading: 🔧 JOB TICKET
blocks.text: A client asked me, completely seriously, whether their router and their modem were the same box with two names. They're not, and knowing the difference — modem, router, switch, NIC, server — is the difference between diagnosing a fault in five minutes or an hour.
Network components for internet connection: server, router, network interface card (NIC), switch, modem

blocks.heading: How to use this lesson
blocks.text: Work through each slide in order. Copy the definitions into your notes. Answer the two practice questions, then mark them yourself with the key.

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Understand the purpose of each network component needed to connect to the internet.
Success criteria

items: Describe the purpose of a modem, router, switch, NIC and server.
Explain how data moves between the components.
Identify the components needed for a network.

blocks.text: Key terms

items.definition: Converts the signal from the service provider's line (e.g. NBN) into data the network can use, and back. For NBN fibre this is often the NBN connection box.
Directs data between the local network and the internet, and gives each device an address. Home routers often include wireless and a switch.
Connects wired devices in a LAN and sends data only to the device it is meant for.
Hardware inside each device that connects it to the network, wired (Ethernet port) or wireless (Wi-Fi).
A computer that provides services to other devices, e.g. storing shared files or running email.

blocks.text: Worked example: Sending a photo from a laptop to the internet

blocks.html:
Follow the data from a laptop in an office.

NIC — The laptop's wireless NIC sends the photo over Wi-Fi.

Router — The router receives it and directs it towards the internet.

Modem — The modem converts it for the provider's line.

Internet — The photo travels to the social media company's servers.

blocks.text: From device to internet

blocks.html:
1

Device + NIC

Connects the device.

2

Switch

Links wired devices together.

3

Router

Directs traffic in and out.

4

Modem — Connects to the provider's line.

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · SPARKY MILLER
blocks.text: Modem connects you to your ISP; router connects your devices to each other and shares that one internet connection. Mix those up in an answer and the marker reads it as not understanding either device, even if the rest of your answer is fine.
Test tip: Router and switch are different

blocks.heading: 🧰 CALLBACK CHECK · SPARKY IS REVIEWING THE JOB
blocks.text: I want the router and modem's roles separated clearly in your answer, not blended into one description. And for 'why does every computer need a NIC' — name what a NIC actually does, don't just say 'to connect to the network'.

That is the router and modem.

Earns full marks — "A switch connects the wired devices within the LAN and sends data only to the device it is addressed to."

blocks.text: Two jobs on my desk this week, same question: wired star or peer-to-peer, client-server or not. The right topology depends entirely on the client's situation — a physio clinic's needs aren't a home network's needs — and that's exactly what the exam wants you to justify, not just define.
Network topologies for local area networks (LANs): wired star, wireless, client server, peer-to-peer

blocks.heading: How to use this lesson
blocks.text: Work through each slide in order. Copy the definitions into your notes. Answer the two practice questions, then mark them yourself with the key.

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Understand the main LAN topologies and network models and when each suits a user.
Success criteria

items: Describe wired star and wireless topologies.
Compare client-server and peer-to-peer networks.
Select a topology for a given situation.

blocks.text: Key terms

items.definition: The layout of how devices are connected in a network.
Every device connects by cable to a central switch. If one cable fails, only that device is affected; if the switch fails, all are.
Devices connect by radio waves to a wireless access point or router.
A central server stores files and controls access; clients request services from it.
All devices are equal and share directly with each other; no central server.

blocks.text: Worked example: Two networks

blocks.html:
A four-person household and a 60-person school admin office.

Household: peer-to-peer, wireless

Few devices, share a printer and files directly, no administrator needed, cheap to set up.

School office: client-server, wired star

Central server stores records, controls who can see what, and backs up every night.

Why star?

A faulty cable only takes one computer offline.

Why wireless too?

Staff laptops and visitors connect without cables.

blocks.text: Client-server vs peer-to-peer

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · SPARKY MILLER
blocks.text: Client-server costs more upfront (you need an actual server) but centralises control and backups — worth it the moment multiple people need shared, managed access to the same data. Peer-to-peer is cheap and simple but falls apart past a handful of devices. Match the answer to the scale of the business, every time.
Test tip: Justify with the scenario

blocks.heading: 🧰 CALLBACK CHECK · SPARKY IS REVIEWING THE JOB
blocks.text: 'Justify' means pick a side and defend it against the client's actual situation. An answer that just describes both options with no recommendation hasn't answered the question, no matter how accurate the description is.

blocks.html:

Earns 0 or 1 mark

"It is good for homes."

No link to this household.

Earns full marks — "With only four people and a few devices, they can share the printer and photos directly without buying a server or needing an administrator, keeping costs low."

blocks.text: The Nguyen family wants their whole house networked and I've got one shot to get the router placement and wiring right before the drywall goes back up. Design a suitable LAN topology for a home network

blocks.heading: How to use this lesson
blocks.text: Work through each slide in order. Copy the definitions into your notes. Answer the two practice questions, then mark them yourself with the key.

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Understand how to design and annotate a LAN for a home using a floor plan.
Success criteria

items: Place network components in suitable locations on a floor plan.
Label each connection as wired or wireless and name the transmission media.
Justify design choices using the scenario.

blocks.text: Key terms

items.definition: Drawing the network on a plan of the building to show where each device and connection goes.
The area the Wi-Fi signal reaches. Walls and distance weaken it; a second access point or mesh unit extends it.
A label naming the device or connection and why it is placed there.

blocks.text: Worked example: The Nguyen family home

blocks.html:
NBN fibre enters at the front of the house. The family has a gaming PC and a smart TV in the lounge, laptops in two bedrooms at the back, and a printer in the study.

Modem and router — At the NBN connection point at the front. Optic fibre from the street.

Wired — Ethernet from the router to a switch in the lounge for the gaming PC and TV: fast and stable for gaming and 4K streaming.

Wireless — Router Wi-Fi covers the front; a mesh unit in the hallway covers the back bedrooms.

Printer — Wireless in the study, so every device can print.

blocks.text: Design checklist

blocks.html:
1

Entry point — Start at the NBN point; place modem and router.

2

Wired devices — Cable fixed, high-use devices; add a switch if needed.

3

Wireless — Check every room is covered; add an access point or mesh unit.

4

Annotate — Label every device, connection (wired/wireless) and medium.

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · SPARKY MILLER
blocks.text: I always put the router as close to centre-of-house as the internet entry point allows, not wherever's convenient to hide the box — coverage dies in corners. And anything that needs a rock-solid, uninterrupted connection — a home office desktop doing video calls — gets a wired run even in an otherwise wireless house.
Test tip: Annotate everything

blocks.heading: 🧰 CALLBACK CHECK · SPARKY IS REVIEWING THE JOB
blocks.text: Annotate the plan like you're handing it to a client who's never seen a floor plan before — placement has to be justified by coverage, not just marked with a dot. And the wired-office-desktop answer needs a reason, not just 'it's better'.

blocks.html:

blocks.heading: 📋 CASE FILE
blocks.text: A ticket seller wants to collect a buyer's school as part of signup and asked me if that's even allowed. Under the Privacy Act 1988 — collection, use, access — the answer is almost never a flat yes or no, it's 'only if it's necessary for the purpose', and most businesses over-collect without realising it.
Role of the Privacy Act 1988 (Australia): collection, use and access of personal information

blocks.heading: How to use this lesson
blocks.text: Work through each slide in order. Copy the definitions into your notes. Answer the two practice questions, then mark them yourself with the key.

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Understand how the Privacy Act 1988 controls the collection, use and access of personal information.
Success criteria

items: State the role of the Privacy Act 1988.
Describe rules for collecting and using personal information.
Describe a person's right to access their information.

blocks.text: Key terms

items.definition: Australian law that regulates how government agencies and most organisations (generally those with turnover over $3 million, plus some smaller ones such as health providers) handle personal information, through the Australian Privacy Principles.
Information that identifies a person or could reasonably identify them: name, address, date of birth, photo, phone number.
Only collect information that is needed, and tell people why it is collected and how it will be used (privacy policy).
Use information for the purpose it was collected for, unless the person agrees or the law allows.
People can ask to see the personal information held about them and ask for it to be corrected.

blocks.text: Worked example: Signing up to a gym app

blocks.html:
A national gym chain asks new members for details in its app.

Collection: OK — Name, email, payment details and emergency contact: needed to run the membership.

Collection: not OK — Religion and income: not needed for gym membership.

Use — Sending class reminders: OK. Selling member emails to a supplement company without consent: not OK.

Access — A member asks for a copy of her data and corrects her old address.

blocks.text: The life of personal information

blocks.html:
1

Collect

Only what is needed; say why.

2

Use

For the stated purpose.

3

Store

Keep it secure.

4

Access — Let people see and correct it.

5

Dispose — Destroy it when no longer needed.

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · DR ELARA FINCH
blocks.text: The test I apply to every collection question: is this piece of personal information actually necessary for what they're using it for? A gym app needs your name and payment details. It very rarely needs your school. If it's not necessary, collecting it is the problem, even if the person consented.
Test tip: Use the correct Act

blocks.heading: 📝 CASE REVIEW · ELARA IS SIGNING OFF
blocks.text: Don't just say 'yes' or 'no' to whether they should collect it — explain it against the necessity test. And for the access right, name it specifically: customers have a right to access their own personal information, which most businesses have to honour on request.

blocks.html:
Question: Describe one requirement of the Privacy Act 1988 when collecting information. (2 marks)

Earns 0 or 1 mark

"They need a good reason."

Too vague; no link to the Act's rules.

Earns full marks — "The organisation must only collect information it needs, and must tell the person why it is collected and how it will be used."

blocks.heading: 📋 CASE FILE
blocks.text: A clinic is replacing its computers and asked me whether they can just put the old ones out for e-waste collection. The answer involves identity theft risk, what counts as a notifiable data breach, and safe disposal — and getting this wrong isn't just an IT mistake, it's a legal one.
Role of the Privacy Act 1988 (Australia): identity theft, safe disposal of data

blocks.heading: How to use this lesson
blocks.text: Work through each slide in order. Copy the definitions into your notes. Answer the two practice questions, then mark them yourself with the key.

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Understand how identity theft happens and how data must be disposed of safely.
Success criteria

items: Describe how identity theft can occur.
Explain the organisation's responsibility to protect and dispose of data.
Describe safe disposal methods.

blocks.text: Key terms

items.definition: Using someone's personal information to pretend to be them, e.g. to open accounts, take loans or make purchases.
Personal information is lost or accessed without permission, e.g. through hacking.
Under the Privacy Act, organisations must tell affected people and the regulator when a breach is likely to cause serious harm.
Destroying or de-identifying personal information when it is no longer needed, so it cannot be recovered.

blocks.text: Worked example: A clinic replaces its computers

blocks.html:
A medical clinic is throwing out five old computers that stored patient records.

Unsafe — Deleting files and putting the computers in a skip. Deleted files can be recovered with free tools.

Safe: wipe — Use data-wiping software that overwrites the whole drive.

Safe: destroy — Remove drives and have them shredded by a certified service.

Paper too — Shred printed records; do not use the recycling bin.

blocks.text: Identity theft

blocks.html:
How it happens

Data breach at a company — Phishing emails and fake websites

Oversharing online (birthday, address, pet names)

Stolen mail or recovered old drives

Reduce the risk

Share only what is needed — Strong, unique passwords and two-step verification

Check bank statements — Securely dispose of old devices and documents

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · DR ELARA FINCH
blocks.text: A data breach only becomes 'notifiable' under the Act when it's likely to cause serious harm — not every leak triggers the same obligations. Knowing that distinction is what separates a business that overreacts to every incident from one that correctly escalates the serious ones.
Test tip: "Delete" is not safe disposal

blocks.heading: 📝 CASE REVIEW · ELARA IS SIGNING OFF
blocks.text: I want stolen data connected to a real, specific identity theft use, not a vague 'they could use it for bad things'. And the retailer's Privacy Act responsibilities need to be named specifically, not summarised as 'they should be careful'.

blocks.html:
Question: Describe one method of safe disposal. (2 marks)

Earns 0 or 1 mark — "Delete the files and empty the recycle bin."

The data can still be recovered. Earns 0.

Earns full marks — "Use data-wiping software to overwrite the entire drive several times, so the old records cannot be recovered."

blocks.heading: 📋 CASE FILE
blocks.text: A council report crossed my desk arguing a new online-only service would 'improve access for everyone' — it wouldn't, and naming exactly who ends up on the wrong side of the digital divide is the whole point of this case. Availability of resources, ability to use them, and dependency on electronic communication are three separate barriers, not one.
Concept of the digital divide and associated issues

blocks.heading: How to use this lesson
blocks.text: Work through each slide in order. Copy the definitions into your notes. Answer the two practice questions, then mark them yourself with the key.

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Understand the digital divide and the issues it creates.
Success criteria

items: Explain the concept of the digital divide.
Describe issues: availability of digital resources, dependency on electronic communication, use of digital technologies, availability of web-based applications.
Explain the effect on a person or group.

blocks.text: Key terms

items.definition: The gap between people who have access to digital technologies and the skills to use them, and people who do not.
Whether people can get devices and a reliable, affordable internet connection.
Whether people have the skills and confidence to use them.
Whether services people need online (banking, government, study) work on their device and connection.
Services moving online-only, which disadvantages people without access.

blocks.text: Worked example: Who is on the wrong side of the divide?

blocks.html:
Four people in the South West.

Farmer, 60 km from town — Slow satellite internet; video calls and uploads often fail.

Pensioner, 82 — Has a phone but not the skills to use myGov or online banking.

Family on a low income — One shared phone and limited data for three school children.

Newly arrived family — Services only in English; websites hard to navigate.

blocks.text: Why it matters now

blocks.html:
Services now mainly online

Banking and bill payment — Government services (myGov, Centrelink)

School work and reports

Job applications — Health appointments (telehealth)

Effects of being left out — Missed information and deadlines

Higher costs (paper bills, travel)

Falling behind at school or work

Social isolation — Relying on others for private matters

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · DR ELARA FINCH
blocks.text: People conflate 'has internet access' with 'digital divide solved' — but someone can have a connection and still be excluded if they lack the skills, the right device, or the confidence to use a service. The divide is about capability as much as access.
Test tip: Link the issue to the person

blocks.heading: 📝 CASE REVIEW · ELARA IS SIGNING OFF
blocks.text: I want the concept defined properly, then the specific groups named for this change — not 'some people will struggle', but which people and why. Elderly residents without a device is a different answer to rural residents with no reliable connection.

blocks.html:
Question: Explain how the digital divide affects the farmer. (3 marks)

Earns 0 or 1 mark

"He has bad internet." — States the issue but not the effect.

Earns full marks — "Slow satellite internet means he cannot reliably use telehealth or upload records to government sites, so he must drive to town, losing a day of work."

blocks.heading: 📋 CASE FILE
blocks.text: A Bunbury surf shop went online this year and the owner's thrilled about 24/7 sales — and surprised by the 2am customer emails expecting instant replies. E-commerce, improved digital communication, round-the-clock trading: every benefit comes with a matched cost, and the exam wants both.
Concept of electronic commerce: implications of improved digital communications, 24/7 communications

blocks.heading: How to use this lesson
blocks.text: Work through each slide in order. Copy the definitions into your notes. Answer the two practice questions, then mark them yourself with the key.

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Understand electronic commerce and the implications of 24/7 digital communication for businesses and customers.
Success criteria

items: Explain the concept of electronic commerce.
Describe implications of improved digital communications.
Explain positive and negative implications of 24/7 communication.

blocks.text: Key terms

items.definition: Buying and selling goods and services over the internet.
Faster internet, mobile devices and apps that let businesses and customers connect instantly.
Customers can shop, message and expect replies at any time of day, every day.
Paying through card, digital wallet or buy now pay later services.

blocks.text: Worked example: A Bunbury surf shop goes online

blocks.html:
The shop adds an online store and Instagram shopping.

Reach — Sells wetsuits to customers across Australia, not only locals.

24/7 sales — Orders arrive at 2 am while the shop is closed.

Expectations — Customers message on Instagram at night and expect quick replies.

New costs — Website fees, packaging, postage and returns.

blocks.text: Implications of 24/7

blocks.html:
For businesses

More sales at any hour — Pressure to reply quickly (chatbots, extra staff)

Competing with global stores on price

Owners find it hard to switch off

For customers

Shop any time, from anywhere

Compare prices easily — Cannot see or try products first

Risk of scams and data theft

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · DR ELARA FINCH
blocks.text: 24/7 availability is the classic double-edged sword in this topic — it genuinely does grow sales outside normal hours, and it genuinely does create an expectation of round-the-clock responsiveness that small operators struggle to meet. Always give both sides unprompted.
Test tip: Implication means a consequence

blocks.heading: 📝 CASE REVIEW · ELARA IS SIGNING OFF
blocks.text: Define e-commerce cleanly first. Then for the 24/7 question, I want one real positive and one real negative — not two positives dressed differently, which is the mistake I see most often.

blocks.html:
Question: Describe one implication of 24/7 communication for a small business. (2 marks)

Earns 0 or 1 mark

"It is always open." — That is the feature, not the consequence.

Earns full marks — "Customers expect replies at night, so the owner must answer messages after hours or pay for a chatbot, adding workload or cost."

blocks.text: A family-owned bakery starts taking online orders for birthday cakes through its website.

blocks.heading: 📋 CASE FILE
blocks.text: A school's systems went down for a day and it exposed exactly how dependent the staff and even the patients at the attached clinic had become on electronic communication. This case is about naming that dependency honestly, and the responsibilities that come with relying on it — including privacy.
Issues related to the dependency of society upon electronic and visual communication

blocks.heading: How to use this lesson
blocks.text: Work through each slide in order. Copy the definitions into your notes. Answer the two practice questions, then mark them yourself with the key.

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Understand the issues that arise when society depends on electronic and visual communication.
Success criteria

items: Describe the requirement for personal development of technology skills.
Describe the responsibility for maintaining privacy when using technology.
Explain an issue for a person or organisation.

blocks.text: Key terms

items.definition: Email, messaging, video calls, social media, images and video used to share information.
Relying on these tools so much that work and daily life cannot happen without them.
People must keep learning new tools to take part in work, study and services.
Each user must protect their own and others' information: settings, passwords, what they share.

blocks.text: Worked example: A school during an outage

blocks.html:
The school's internet goes down for a full day.

Learning — Lessons, assessments and notes are all online: classes cannot run as planned.

Communication — Staff cannot email parents; the school uses a phone tree.

Admin — Attendance and canteen orders are recorded on paper.

Lesson learned — Keep offline backups and a plan for outages.

blocks.text: Two key issues

blocks.html:
Technology skills — Jobs need new software skills every few years

Older workers may need retraining

Services assume users can use apps

Schools must teach digital skills

Maintaining privacy — Screenshots can be shared without permission

Location data in photos — Video calls can show private spaces

Users must set privacy and security settings

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · DR ELARA FINCH
blocks.text: Dependency isn't automatically a flaw to criticise — it's a fact to manage. The useful answer isn't 'people shouldn't rely on technology so much', it's identifying the specific skill gap or responsibility that the outage exposed, and what closes that gap.
Test tip: Name the issue and explain it

blocks.heading: 📝 CASE REVIEW · ELARA IS SIGNING OFF
blocks.text: Name the actual skill staff and patients need to develop, not a generic 'get better with tech'. And the privacy responsibility question wants a specific duty — what they're responsible for maintaining, and why it's on them, not just the provider.

blocks.html:
Question: Explain one issue of society's dependency on electronic communication. (3 marks)

Earns 0 or 1 mark

"People use phones too much."

Not linked to an issue in the syllabus.

Earns full marks — "Workers need to keep learning new tools, such as a new booking system, so staff without training are left behind or need retraining, which costs the business time."

blocks.text: A medical centre moves all appointments, reminders and test results to an app. Staff now talk to patients mainly by video call.

blocks.heading: 🎟️ TICKET
blocks.text: Three students planning the Year 12 formal are scattered across different towns and need to actually get work done together, not just message about it. Choosing the right collaboration tools — and being honest about the real downside — is the difference between a project that moves and one stuck in a group chat forever.
Types of online collaboration

blocks.heading: How to use this lesson
blocks.text: Work through each slide in order. Copy the definitions into your notes. Answer the two practice questions, then mark them yourself with the key.

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Understand the types of online collaboration and when each is useful.
Success criteria

items: Identify types of online collaboration.
Describe how each type supports a team.
Explain advantages and disadvantages of online collaboration.

blocks.text: Key terms

rows: People working together on the same task using internet-based tools.
Several people edit the same file at the same time.
Live meetings with video and audio.
Storing files online so the team can access them.
Feedback attached to parts of a file, and a record of changes.

blocks.text: Worked example: Planning a Year 12 formal

blocks.html:
A committee of six students across three classes organises the formal.

Shared document — Budget sheet edited by everyone, so there is one current version.

Chat — Quick questions about the venue in a Teams channel.

Video call — Weekly 15-minute meeting on Teams, since members are in different classes.

Comments — Teacher adds comments on the theme proposal instead of emailing a new file.

blocks.text: Online collaboration

blocks.html:
Advantages

Work from anywhere, any time

Everyone sees the latest version

Changes are tracked

Less travel and printing

Disadvantages — Needs a reliable internet connection

Easy to overwrite others' work without version control

Messages can be misunderstood

Some members may not contribute

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · RORY QUINN
blocks.text: The disadvantage question is the one everyone skips, because collaboration tools feel like an unqualified good. They're not — version confusion, unequal contribution, or someone's patchy wifi dropping them from a call are all real costs, and naming one honestly is worth more than pretending collaboration has no downside.
Test tip: Name the type, then the benefit

blocks.heading: 🛑 STANDUP REVIEW · RORY IS CHECKING THE BOARD
blocks.text: Describe two distinct types of collaboration this group could actually use — not two tools that do the same job. And the disadvantage needs to be a genuine cost of collaborating remotely, not a generic complaint about technology.

blocks.html:

Earns 0 or 1 mark

"Teams." — A product name, not a type, and no description.

Earns full marks — "Co-authoring a shared budget sheet in OneDrive, so all six members update one file and always see the latest figures."

blocks.heading: 🎟️ TICKET
blocks.text: A small club website needs a colour scheme change and what should've been a five-minute job turned into editing forty separate pages — because nobody used a .css file. Hyperlinks, templates, .htm versus .css — knowing what each piece is actually for would have saved this entire sprint.
Features of web authoring: hyperlinks, graphics, templates, types of files (.css, .htm/.html)

blocks.heading: How to use this lesson
blocks.text: Work through each slide in order. Copy the definitions into your notes. Answer the two practice questions, then mark them yourself with the key.

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Understand the main features of web authoring and the files that make up a website.
Success criteria

items: Describe hyperlinks, graphics and templates.
Explain the purpose of .html and .css files.
Use web authoring features in a product.

blocks.text: Key terms

items.definition: Clickable text or image that goes to another page, part of a page, file or email address.
Images, logos and icons on a web page, usually JPEG, PNG or SVG, optimised for fast loading.
A pre-designed layout reused on every page for consistency.
HyperText Markup Language: holds the content and structure of a page (headings, text, links, images).
Cascading Style Sheet: controls how pages look (colours, fonts, layout). One CSS file can style every page.

blocks.text: Worked example: Inside a small website

blocks.html:
A three-page site for a local cafe.

index.html, menu.html, contact.html

Content and structure of each page.

style.css — One file sets the brand colours and fonts for all three pages.

Hyperlinks — Menu bar links each page; a "mailto:" link opens an email; a link to the Google Maps location.

Template — Same header, menu and footer on every page.

blocks.text: Why separate HTML and CSS?

blocks.html:
HTML: what is on the page

Headings and paragraphs

Images and alt text

Hyperlinks

Lists and tables

CSS: how it looks — Change the brand colour once and every page updates

Consistent fonts and spacing (unity)

Different layouts for phones and laptops

Smaller files, faster loading

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · RORY QUINN
blocks.text: A .css file is the single highest-leverage thing in basic web authoring — one file controls the look of every page that links to it. Any site that doesn't use one is signing up for exactly the pain this club just went through, and it's completely avoidable.
Test tip: Say what the file does

blocks.heading: 🛑 STANDUP REVIEW · RORY IS CHECKING THE BOARD
blocks.text: Describe two distinct hyperlink types the club site could actually use — internal, external, email, download — not two examples of the same type. And explain the .css benefit against this exact colour-change problem, not css in the abstract.

blocks.html:
Question: Describe the purpose of a .css file. (2 marks)

Earns 0 or 1 mark

"It is a web file."

Too general.

Earns full marks — "A .css file stores the styles, such as colours and fonts, for the whole website, so changing one rule updates every page."

blocks.text: A student builds a five-page website for a netball club. Each page has its colours and fonts set inside the HTML, and the club now wants to change its brand colour.

blocks.heading: 🚀 SPRINT CHALLENGE
blocks.text: Describe two hyperlink types for the club website, and how a .css file would have made the colour change easier, before you check my fix.

blocks.title: Build a Three-Page Site With a Shared Stylesheet
blocks.software: Any text editor (e.g. VS Code) and a browser
blocks.intro: Build the exact fix the club website in this lesson needed — a shared .css file — so one colour change updates every page at once.
steps: Create three files: index.html, about.html and contact.html, each with a heading and a short paragraph.

blocks.text: A camping app needs its navigation planned before a single screen gets built — hierarchical, linear, or networked structure, and the choice has to match how people actually use a camping app, not just what looks tidy on paper.
Create a navigation map

blocks.text: Work through each slide in order. Copy the definitions into your notes. Answer the two practice questions, then mark them yourself with the key.

blocks.text: Understand how to plan the pages and links of a digital product with a navigation map.
Success criteria

items: Describe the purpose of a navigation map.
Identify linear, hierarchical and networked structures.
Draw a navigation map for a product.

blocks.text: Key terms

items.definition: A diagram of every page or screen in a product and the links between them.
Pages branch from a home page into sections, like a family tree.
Pages follow one after another in a set order (Next, Back).
Pages link to many other pages, not in a fixed order.

blocks.text: Worked example: Navigation map for a camping app

blocks.html:
An app with a Home screen, Campsites, Bookings and Help.

Level 1

Home.

Drawing it — Boxes for screens, lines for links, arrows show direction; label every link.

blocks.text: Choosing a structure

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · RORY QUINN
blocks.text: Linear structures suit a fixed sequence a user has to follow — a checkout flow, a tutorial. Hierarchical suits browsing categories, which is exactly what a camping app needs: parks, then sites, then details. Pick the structure the user's actual task demands, not the one that's easiest to diagram.
Test tip: Every page, every link

blocks.heading: 🛑 STANDUP REVIEW · RORY IS CHECKING THE BOARD
blocks.text: Identify the structure and justify it against how people actually browse camping sites, not against structure in the abstract. And the navigation map features need to be concrete — what's actually shown on each level — not a vague description.

blocks.heading: 🎟️ TICKET
blocks.text: A news site looks perfect on a desktop and falls apart on a phone — overlapping text, a menu that eats half the screen. Responsive design — fluid grids, flexible images, breakpoints, the hamburger menu — exists purely to stop exactly this from happening, and it's non-negotiable on any public-facing site in 2026.
Concept of responsive design

blocks.heading: How to use this lesson
blocks.text: Work through each slide in order. Copy the definitions into your notes. Answer the two practice questions, then mark them yourself with the key.

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Understand how responsive design lets one product work on phones, tablets and computers.
Success criteria

items: Explain the concept of responsive design.
Describe techniques used in responsive design.
Explain why responsive design matters for users.

blocks.text: Key terms

items.definition: Designing a web page or product so its layout automatically adjusts to the screen size and device.
Columns sized in percentages, so they stretch or shrink with the screen.
Images that scale down to fit the screen width.
A screen width where the layout changes, e.g. three columns become one on a phone.
A three-line icon that opens the menu on small screens to save space.

blocks.text: Worked example: One news site, three screens

blocks.html:
The same home page on three devices.

Desktop — Three columns of stories; full menu across the top.

Tablet — Two columns; menu still visible.

Phone — One column; menu collapses to a hamburger icon; buttons large enough to tap.

What stays the same — Content, colours and fonts, so the brand is consistent.

blocks.text: Why it matters

blocks.html:
For users

No pinching and zooming

Buttons easy to tap

Faster loading on mobile data

Same content on every device

For the business

Most visitors now use phones

One site to maintain, not two

Search engines rank mobile-friendly sites higher

Fewer users leave the site

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · RORY QUINN
blocks.text: A breakpoint isn't a fixed rule you memorise once — it's wherever the current layout actually starts to break for a given screen width, and that's different for every design. Test on the real device, don't guess the number from a textbook.
Test tip: Concept means explain the idea

blocks.heading: 🛑 STANDUP REVIEW · RORY IS CHECKING THE BOARD
blocks.text: Explain the concept properly — layout adapting to screen size — before diagnosing this specific site's problems. And I want two concrete responsive fixes for this exact news site, not a generic list of responsive techniques.

blocks.html:
Question: Explain the concept of responsive design. (2 marks)

Earns 0 or 1 mark

"It works on phones."

Does not explain how.

Earns full marks — "The layout automatically adjusts to the screen size, e.g. three columns on a laptop become one on a phone, so content is easy to read on any device."

blocks.text: A cafe website shows a wide menu table and small buttons. On a phone, customers have to zoom in and scroll sideways.

blocks.heading: 🚀 SPRINT CHALLENGE
blocks.text: Explain responsive design, then describe two fixes for the news site on a small screen, before you check my audit.

blocks.title: Make a Page Actually Responsive
blocks.software: Any text editor and a browser
blocks.intro: Take a simple page and deliberately break it on a small screen first, then fix it with real responsive techniques — not by guessing, by testing.
steps: Build a simple HTML page with a header, a navigation menu with 5 links, and a 3-column layout of content using fixed pixel widths (e.g. three divs each width: 400px).
Open your browser's device toolbar (F12 then the device icon, or Ctrl+Shift+M) and switch to a phone-width view.
Note what breaks — likely horizontal scrolling and overlapping columns.
Fix the columns using a fluid, percentage-based or flexbox/grid layout instead of fixed pixel widths.
Add a CSS media query breakpoint that stacks the columns vertically below 600px width.
Replace the 5-link navigation menu with a hamburger menu (a simple toggle button that shows/hides the links) that appears only below the same breakpoint.
Re-test at phone width and confirm there's no horizontal scrolling and the menu toggles correctly.

blocks.heading: 🎟️ TICKET
blocks.text: A bouncing ball animation and a logo that needs to move — frames, keyframes, tweening, buttons. Simple-sounding brief, but 'simple' animation is where most students lose marks explaining the mechanics instead of just describing what they saw happen.
Features of animation software: frame by frame, tweens, buttons

blocks.heading: How to use this lesson
blocks.text: Work through each slide in order. Copy the definitions into your notes. Answer the two practice questions, then mark them yourself with the key.

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Understand the main features of animation software and when to use each.
Success criteria

items: Describe frame by frame animation and tweens.
Compare frame by frame and tweened animation.
Describe how buttons make an animation interactive.

blocks.text: Key terms

items.definition: One still image in an animation. Frame rate is frames per second (fps).
A frame where something important changes, such as a start or end position.
Every frame is drawn or changed by hand. Detailed but slow to make.
The software creates the frames between two keyframes automatically, e.g. a motion or shape tween.
An interactive object that responds to the user (up, over, down states) and triggers an action.

blocks.text: Worked example: Animating a bouncing ball

blocks.html:
Two ways to make a ball bounce across the screen.

Frame by frame — Draw the ball in 24 positions for 1 second at 24 fps. Can add squash and stretch by hand.

Motion tween — Set the start and end keyframes; the software fills in the frames between.

Shape tween — The ball changes into a star over 12 frames.

Button — A Play button starts the animation when clicked.

blocks.text: Frame by frame vs tween

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · RORY QUINN
blocks.text: A tween isn't magic — it's the software calculating every frame between two keyframes you set manually. If you can't explain that a tween needs a start keyframe and an end keyframe to interpolate between, you don't yet understand why it works, you've just used the button.
Test tip: Compare means both sides on each feature

blocks.heading: 🛑 STANDUP REVIEW · RORY IS CHECKING THE BOARD
blocks.text: Describe the tween specifically for the logo movement — what moves, between which two states — not just 'a tween was used'. And the button question wants its purpose and its states (up, over, down) both covered, not just 'it's clickable'.

blocks.html:
Question: Compare frame by frame and tweened animation. (4 marks)

Earns 0 or 1 mark

"Tweening is faster."

One side of one feature.

Earns full marks — "Tweening is faster because the software creates the in-between frames, while frame by frame is slower but gives full control over every movement."

blocks.text: A student is making an animated title for a school video: the school logo slides in from the left and fades in, then a "Watch now" button appears.

blocks.heading: 🚀 SPRINT CHALLENGE
blocks.text: Describe how a tween could create the logo movement, and a button's purpose and states, before you check my breakdown.

blocks.title: Animate a Bouncing Ball With Tweens
blocks.software: Any animation tool with keyframes (e.g. Canva, Adobe Animate, or CSS animation in a browser)
blocks.intro: Build the exact animation from this lesson's worked example — a ball that bounces — using real keyframes and tweening, not a pre-made GIF.
steps: Create a canvas or frame roughly 400×400px with a simple circle as your ball.
Set a keyframe with the ball at the top of the frame.
Set a second keyframe a short time later with the ball at the bottom of the frame.
Apply a tween between the two keyframes and preview it — confirm the software is calculating the frames in between, not that you drew them.
Add a third keyframe that squashes the ball slightly wider and shorter at the moment it hits the bottom, for a more realistic bounce.
Add a simple button (even just a shape) elsewhere in the frame with at least two states — e.g. a different fill colour for 'up' and 'over'.
Export the animation as a GIF or short video.
Write one sentence identifying the start keyframe and end keyframe your tween used.

1 mark – States the software moves the logo

question.explanation: 3 marks – Describes that a button lets the user interact and triggers an action (1), and names the states up, over, down (1 each, up to 2)

blocks.text: A band wants a website and handed me a vague list of 'things to do' with no order and no dates — not a plan, just a wish list. A real plan of action needs every task, every milestone, every dependency laid out, or the project drifts the moment anything gets busy.
Project management techniques: plan of action

blocks.heading: How to use this lesson
blocks.text: Work through each slide in order. Copy the definitions into your notes. Answer the two practice questions, then mark them yourself with the key.

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Understand what a plan of action is and how to write one for a digital project.
Success criteria

items: Describe the purpose of a plan of action.
Identify the parts of a plan of action.
Write a plan of action for a project.

blocks.text: Key terms

items.definition: A document listing every task in order, with the time allocated, resources needed, who is responsible and the due date.
One piece of work that can be completed and checked, e.g. "draw five wireframes".
A key point in the project, e.g. design approved by client.
A task that cannot start until another is finished.

blocks.text: Worked example: Plan of action: a band's website

blocks.html:
A student is building a three-page website for a local band in four weeks.

Week 1 — Interview band (1 hr, notebook); research 2 band sites (1 hr); navigation map (30 min).

Week 2 — Wireframes for 3 pages (2 hrs, paper); band approves design (milestone).

Week 3 — Build pages (4 hrs, laptop, web software, band photos).

Week 4 — Test on phone and laptop (1 hr); band feedback; final changes; publish.

blocks.text: Parts of a plan of action

rows: Draw wireframes for all three pages

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · RORY QUINN
blocks.text: Dependencies are what separate a task list from a plan. If 'build the gallery page' depends on 'collect band photos' finishing first, and you don't mark that dependency, someone will start the gallery with no photos and waste the sprint. Always ask what has to happen before this.
Test tip: Tasks must be specific

blocks.heading: 🛑 STANDUP REVIEW · RORY IS CHECKING THE BOARD
blocks.text: I want all four parts in every row — task, time, who's responsible, and dependency — not three out of four. And the three tasks you write need a real time estimate each, not 'soon' or 'later'.

blocks.html:
Question: Describe the purpose of a plan of action. (2 marks)

Earns 0 or 1 mark

"To plan the project." — Repeats the words in the question.

Earns full marks — "It breaks the project into ordered tasks with times and due dates, so the designer can check progress and finish by the deadline."

blocks.text: A student has three weeks to design and print a program for the school musical. The drama teacher must approve the design before printing.

blocks.intro: Turn the band website brief from this lesson into an actual plan of action with every required part in every row.

List at least eight tasks needed to build a simple band website, in a logical order (e.g. 'collect band photos' before 'build the gallery page').
For every task, fill in a realistic time estimate and a responsible person (use fictional names if working alone).
For every task, name its dependency — which earlier task must finish first — or write 'none' if it has no dependency.
Highlight the longest chain of dependent tasks (the critical path) in one colour.
Add one milestone row marking 'Website live' at the end, with its own target date.
Save the file as band-website-plan-of-action.

blocks.heading: 🎟️ TICKET
blocks.text: A project's running late and the team's panicking instead of triaging. Prioritising, milestones, a Gantt chart, buffer time, time blocking — this is the rescue kit, and knowing which tool actually fixes a late project versus which one just looks organised matters right now.
Project management techniques: time management strategies

blocks.heading: How to use this lesson
blocks.text: Work through each slide in order. Copy the definitions into your notes. Answer the two practice questions, then mark them yourself with the key.

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Understand strategies that help a project finish on time.
Success criteria

items: Describe time management strategies.
Select strategies suited to a project.
Explain how a strategy helps meet a deadline.

blocks.text: Key terms

items.definition: Doing the most important or urgent tasks first.
Breaking the project into checkpoints with dates, so progress can be checked.
A bar chart showing each task against time, so overlaps and delays are easy to see.
Extra time left before the deadline for problems and changes.
Setting aside fixed time slots for particular tasks.

blocks.text: Worked example: Rescuing a late project

blocks.html:
A designer has a week left to finish a client's logo and business cards, but has only done research.

Prioritise — Logo first: the business cards depend on it.

Milestones — Logo sketches by Tuesday; client approval Wednesday; cards by Friday.

Time block — Two hours every morning with notifications turned off.

Buffer — Keep Friday afternoon free for client changes.

blocks.text: Time wasters and fixes

blocks.html:
Time wasters

Starting with the fun task

Waiting until the night before

Phone notifications while working

Redoing work because the brief was not checked

Fixes — Prioritise by dependency and deadline

Milestones with dates — Time blocks with notifications off

Check the brief and get approval early

blocks.heading: 💡 SENIOR WISDOM · RORY QUINN
blocks.text: Buffer time isn't slack for being lazy — it's the only thing standing between 'one task runs long' and 'the whole project misses its deadline'. A plan with zero buffer is a plan that was already late the moment anything went even slightly wrong.
Test tip: Link the strategy to the project

blocks.heading: 🛑 STANDUP REVIEW · RORY IS CHECKING THE BOARD
blocks.text: Describe two strategies that would actually rescue this specific late project, not two generic time management tips. And explain why buffer time matters here specifically — what it protects against — not 'it's good practice'.

blocks.html:
Question: Describe one time management strategy for the logo project. (2 marks)

Earns 0 or 1 mark

"Manage your time well."

Not a strategy.

Earns full marks — "Set a milestone for client approval on Wednesday, so there is time to fix problems before the cards are due on Friday."

blocks.text: Two students are making a five-minute documentary for a local museum in four weeks. They keep running out of class time and have not started editing.

blocks.heading: 🚀 SPRINT CHALLENGE

blocks.title: Build a Gantt Chart to Rescue a Late Project
blocks.software: Microsoft Excel, Google Sheets, or a dedicated Gantt tool
blocks.intro: Build an actual Gantt chart for the late project from this lesson, with real buffer time included — not just a task list.
steps: List at least six tasks for a simple project of your choice (e.g. producing a short video) down the left column.
Across the top, add column headers for each day or week of the project timeline.
For each task, shade the cells spanning the days it will take, showing tasks that overlap and tasks that depend on earlier ones finishing first.
Add at least one buffer block (a shaded cell explicitly labelled 'Buffer') before the final deadline.
Mark today's date with a vertical line or highlighted column.
Write two sentences: one naming a time management strategy you used building this (prioritising, milestones, time blocking) and one explaining what the buffer protects against.

blocks.text: A community garden newsletter's done and now it needs evaluating properly — product, process, a user survey, client feedback — before anyone can honestly say whether it worked, or just assume it did because it got finished.
Project management techniques: evaluation

blocks.heading: How to use this lesson
blocks.text: Work through each slide in order. Copy the definitions into your notes. Answer the two practice questions, then mark them yourself with the key.

blocks.heading: Lesson objective
blocks.text: Understand how to evaluate a finished product and the project process.
Success criteria

items: Describe evaluation tools: user survey, client feedback, self-reflection.
Evaluate a product against design criteria with evidence.
Review a plan of action and recommend improvements.

blocks.text: Key terms

items.definition: Judging how well the finished product meets the brief and design criteria.
Judging how well the project was managed: time, resources and the plan of action.
Questions for users, including rating scales and open questions.
The client's written comments on whether the brief has been met.
A specific change to make next time.

blocks.text: Worked example: Evaluating a community garden newsletter

blocks.html:
A student made a 4-page digital newsletter for a community garden.

Survey (12 members) — 10 of 12 found the planting calendar useful; 5 said the text was too small on phones.

Client feedback — The coordinator said the working-bee date was missing from page 1.

Self-reflection — The layout met the grid criterion; the font size criterion was not met.

Process — Photos took a week longer than planned. Next time: book the photographer in week 1.

blocks.text: Evaluation frame

rows: Add a dates box to page 1

Test tip: Evidence, not opinion

blocks.heading: 🛑 STANDUP REVIEW · RORY IS CHECKING THE BOARD
blocks.text: Name two real tools for gathering evaluation evidence — a survey, direct feedback — not 'I would ask people how it went'. And the recommendation for next time needs to be specific and actionable, not 'do better next time'.

Question: Evaluate the product against one design criterion. (3 marks)

Earns 0 or 1 mark — "I think it is really good and the client liked it."

No criterion, no evidence.

Earns full marks — "Criterion: readable on a phone. Partly met: 5 of 12 surveyed members said the text was too small. Increasing body text to 14 pt would fix this."

blocks.title: Evaluate the Community Garden Newsletter
blocks.software: Any word processor, plus a survey tool (e.g. Google Forms) if available
blocks.intro: Produce both a product evaluation and a process evaluation for the community garden newsletter from this lesson — two different questions, two different kinds of evidence.
steps: Find or create a simple one-page newsletter (any topic is fine if you don't have a real one).
Write three product evaluation criteria (does the finished newsletter meet the brief — e.g. readable font size, all sections present, fits on one page).
Write two process evaluation questions (did the way the team worked go smoothly — e.g. was the deadline met, did everyone contribute).
Create a short 3-question survey (Google Forms or on paper) asking a reader to rate the newsletter against your product criteria.
Collect at least two responses and summarise the feedback in one paragraph.
Recommend one specific, actionable change for next time's newsletter based on the feedback.
